public class MacCheckbox implements Checkbox {
    @Override
    public void render() {
        System.out.println("Rendering Mac Checkbox");
    }
}

5. Client Code:

public class Application {
    private GUIFactory factory;
    private Button button;
    private Checkbox checkbox;

    public Application(GUIFactory factory) {
        this.factory = factory;
    }

    public void createUI() {
        button = factory.createButton();
        checkbox = factory.createCheckbox();
    }

    public void render() {
        button.render();
        checkbox.render();
    }
}

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        GUIFactory factory;
        String os = System.getProperty("os.name").toLowerCase();

        if (os.contains("win")) {
            factory = new WindowsFactory();
        } else {
            factory = new MacFactory();
        }

        Application app = new Application(factory);
        app.createUI();
        app.render();
    }
}

Advantages

  1. Encapsulation of Families: Groups related product creation logic in one place.
  2. Consistency: Ensures that all products in a family are compatible.
  3. Open/Closed Principle: Adding new product families requires creating new factories without modifying existing code.
  4. Ease of Testing: Abstract factories can be mocked or stubbed for unit testing.

Disadvantages

  1. Complexity: Introduces additional classes and interfaces, increasing complexity.
  2. Rigid Design: Adding new product types (not families) requires changes to the factory interfaces and all implementations.

Comparison with related patterns

Aspect

Factory Method

Abstract Factory

Focus

Creates one type of object

Creates families of related objects

Complexity

Simpler

More complex

Extensibility

Easy to add new product types

Easy to add new product families

Best practices

  1. Group Related Products: Use the pattern to encapsulate logic for families of objects that must work together.
  2. Ensure Consistency: Validate that products created by the factory belong to the same family.
  3. Use Dependency Injection: Inject the abstract factory into the client for greater flexibility.
  4. Avoid Overuse: Use Abstract Factory only when the complexity of object creation justifies its overhead.

Examples

  1. Cross-Platform UI Toolkits: GUI frameworks like Qt or Swing use Abstract Factory to create platform-specific components.
  2. Themed Applications: Applications that switch between themes use Abstract Factory to provide theme-specific components.
  3. Database Drivers: Abstract Factory can be used to create database connections for different vendors (e.g., MySQL, PostgreSQL).


Singletion pattern

The Singleton pattern is a creational design pattern that ensures a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access to that instance. It is one of the simplest yet most controversial design patterns due to its potential for misuse.

1. What is the Singleton Pattern?

The Singleton pattern:

  • Restricts instantiation of a class to a single object.
  • Provides a global point of access to the instance.
  • Is useful when exactly one object is required to coordinate actions across the system.

2. Key Characteristics of the Singleton Pattern

  1. Single Instance:

    • Only one instance of the class exists during the application's lifecycle.

  2. Global Access Point:

    • The instance is accessible globally through a static method or property.

  3. Lazy Initialization (Optional):

    • The instance is created only when it is first accessed, saving resources.

3. Benefits of the Singleton Pattern

  1. Controlled Access to the Instance:

    • Centralized control over object creation.

  2. Global State Management:

    • Provides a global, shared state that all parts of the application can access.

  3. Resource Efficiency:

    • Prevents the overhead of creating multiple instances.

  4. Consistent Behavior:

    • Ensures all parts of the application work with the same instance.

4. Challenges and Drawbacks of the Singleton Pattern

  1. Global State:

    • Can lead to unexpected side effects and make debugging difficult.

  2. Testability:

    • Singleton instances are hard to mock or replace in unit tests.

  3. Violation of SOLID Principles:

    • Often violates the Single Responsibility Principle by controlling its own lifecycle and global access.

  4. Concurrency Issues:

    • Improper implementation can lead to race conditions in multi-threaded environments.

5. How the Singleton Pattern Works

  1. Private Constructor:

    • Prevents external instantiation.

  2. Static Instance Variable:

    • Holds the single instance of the class.

  3. Public Access Method:

    • Provides a global point of access to the instance.

  4. Thread Safety (Optional):

    • Ensures the pattern works correctly in multi-threaded applications.

6. Implementation Examples

1. Basic Singleton in Java

Code:

java
Copy code
public class Singleton {
    private static Singleton instance;

    // Private constructorprivate Singleton() {}

    // Public access methodpublic static Singleton getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {
            instance = new Singleton();
        }
        return instance;
    }
}

Usage:

java
Copy code
Singleton singleton = Singleton.getInstance();

2. Thread-Safe Singleton

Code:

java
Copy code
public class Singleton {
    private static Singleton instance;

    private Singleton() {}

    public static synchronized Singleton getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {
            instance = new Singleton();
        }
        return instance;
    }
}

3. Double-Checked Locking

Improves performance by minimizing synchronization overhead.

Code:

java
Copy code
public class Singleton {
    private static volatile Singleton instance;

    private Singleton() {}

    public static Singleton getInstance() {
        if (instance == null) {
            synchronized (Singleton.class) {
                if (instance == null) {
                    instance = new Singleton();
                }
            }
        }
        return instance;
    }
}

4. Singleton with Lazy Initialization

Code:

java
Copy code
public class Singleton {
    private static class SingletonHelper {
        private static final Singleton INSTANCE = new Singleton();
    }

    private Singleton() {}

    public static Singleton getInstance() {
        return SingletonHelper.INSTANCE;
    }
}

5. Enum-Based Singleton (Thread-Safe by Design)

The simplest and safest implementation in Java.

Code:

java
Copy code
public enum Singleton {
    INSTANCE;

    public void doSomething() {
        System.out.println("Singleton instance is doing something.");
    }
}

Usage:

java
Copy code
Singleton.INSTANCE.doSomething();

7. Common Use Cases for the Singleton Pattern

  1. Configuration Management:

    • Managing application-wide settings or configuration values.

  2. Logging:

    • Providing a global logging instance.

  3. Resource Management:

    • Managing shared resources such as thread pools, database connections, or file access.

  4. Caching:

    • Storing frequently accessed data in a globally available cache.

  5. Service Locator:

    • Centralized registry for service instances.

8. Best Practices for Using the Singleton Pattern

  1. Limit Usage:

    • Avoid using singletons as a default solution for global state.

  2. Thread Safety:

    • Ensure thread-safe implementation, especially in multi-threaded applications.

  3. Dependency Injection:

    • Prefer dependency injection over singletons for better testability and flexibility.

  4. Avoid Overuse:

    • Use the singleton pattern only when a single instance is genuinely required.

  5. Consider Alternatives:

    • For managing global state, consider alternatives like context objects or dependency injection containers.

10. Real-World Examples

  1. Java:

    • The Runtime class in Java is implemented as a singleton.

  2. Spring Framework:

    • The default scope of Spring beans (Singleton) ensures a single instance per application context.

  3. .NET:

    • The HttpContext in ASP.NET Core often follows a singleton pattern for global request handling.


Prototype pattern

What it is?

The Prototype pattern is a creational design pattern that enables the creation of new objects by copying existing ones, rather than instantiating them directly. It is particularly useful when object creation is resource-intensive, or when a large number of objects share similar initial configurations.


The Prototype pattern:

  • Relies on cloning to create new objects.
  • Avoids the cost of creating new objects from scratch.
  • Allows for dynamic configuration of objects during runtime.

Key characteristics

  1. Cloning: New objects are created by copying the structure and data of existing objects. Implemented through a clone or similar method.
  2. Decoupling: Decouples object instantiation from client code.
  3. Dynamic Object Creation: Enables object creation at runtime, based on the current state of another object.

Benefits

  1. Performance: Reduces the cost of creating new instances, especially for complex objects.
  2. Flexibility: New objects can be created without knowing the exact class of the object.
  3. Runtime Configuration: Allows objects to be configured dynamically and reused as prototypes.
  4. Simplified Object Creation: Eliminates the need for a separate factory for complex initialization logic.

Challenges

  1. Deep vs. Shallow Cloning: Handling nested objects can be complex. A shallow clone copies references, while a deep clone copies all nested objects.
  2. Implementation Complexity: Requires implementing a cloning mechanism, which may be non-trivial for objects with complex dependencies.
  3. State Management: Managing the state of cloned objects can become cumbersome in large systems.

How it works

  1. Prototype Interface: Defines the clone method for copying objects.
  2. Concrete Prototype: Implements the cloning logic.
  3. Client: Requests new objects by cloning existing ones.

Implementation

1. Prototype Interface

Code:

public interface Prototype {
    Prototype clone();
}

2. Concrete Prototype

Code:

public class Circle implements Prototype {
    private int radius;
    private String color;

    public Circle(int radius, String color) {
        this.radius = radius;
        this.color = color;
    }

    public void setRadius(int radius) {
        this.radius = radius;
    }

    public void setColor(String color) {
        this.color = color;
    }

    @Override
    public Circle clone() {
        return new Circle(this.radius, this.color);
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "Circle [radius=" + radius + ", color=" + color + "]";
    }
}

3. Usage Example

Code:

public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Circle prototype = new Circle(10, "Red");
        System.out.println("Original: " + prototype);

        Circle clone1 = prototype.clone();
        clone1.setColor("Blue");

        System.out.println("Clone 1: " + clone1);
        System.out.println("Original: " + prototype);
    }
}

Output:

plaintext
Copy code
Original: Circle [radius=10, color=Red]
Clone 1: Circle [radius=10, color=Blue]
Original: Circle [radius=10, color=Red]

4. Deep Cloning

For nested objects, implement deep cloning by recursively cloning all dependent objects.

Code:

public class Rectangle implements Prototype {
    private Point topLeft;
    private int width;
    private int height;

    public Rectangle(Point topLeft, int width, int height) {
        this.topLeft = topLeft;
        this.width = width;
        this.height = height;
    }

    @Override
    public Rectangle clone() {
        return new Rectangle(new Point(this.topLeft.getX(), this.topLeft.getY()), this.width, this.height);
    }
}

Use cases

  1. Complex Object Initialization: When creating new objects involves expensive operations like database queries or complex computations.
  2. Dynamic Object Configuration: When objects need to be dynamically configured and reused.
  3. Gaming: Reusing game objects like enemies, power-ups, or map tiles.
  4. Prototyping in Applications: Creating sample objects with preset configurations for quick instantiation.

Advantages

  1. Efficient Object Creation: Avoids redundant initialization logic.
  2. Encapsulation of Cloning Logic: Centralizes cloning in the prototype class, reducing code duplication.
  3. Dynamic Runtime Behavior: Supports creating objects dynamically based on existing state.

Disadvantages

  1. Complexity in Deep Cloning: Implementing deep cloning for complex object hierarchies can be error-prone.
  2. Copy Semantics: Requires careful consideration of how attributes are copied (e.g., mutable vs. immutable fields).

Comparison with related patterns

Aspect

Prototype

Factory

Singleton

Purpose

Creates objects by cloning

Encapsulates object creation logic

Ensures a single instance

Creation Method

Cloning

Instantiation

Controlled within the Singleton

Use Case

Reuse existing state for new objects

Centralize and abstract creation

Manage global state

Examples

  1. Document Cloning: Applications like Microsoft Word use prototypes for duplicating documents with the same formatting.
  2. Game Development: Reusing game entities like NPCs, enemies, or items.
  3. UI Elements: Reusing UI components with the same properties in GUI frameworks.

Best practices

  1. Choose Between Shallow and Deep Cloning: Use shallow cloning for simple objects and deep cloning for complex, nested structures.
  2. Implement Cloning Carefully: Ensure cloned objects are independent of the original to avoid unintended side effects.
  3. Use Immutable Objects: When possible, design prototypes with immutable properties to simplify cloning.
  4. Combine with Factory Patterns: Use a factory to manage prototypes for even greater flexibility.


Builder pattern

What it is?

The Builder pattern is a creational design pattern that provides a structured way to construct complex objects step by step. It allows for creating different representations of an object using the same construction process, making it ideal for creating objects with multiple configurations.


The Builder pattern:

  • Separates the construction logic of an object from its representation.
  • Provides a way to construct a complex object step by step.
  • Enables the creation of various representations of the same object.

Key characteristics

  1. Step-by-Step Construction: Constructs the object incrementally through defined steps.
  2. Encapsulation of Construction Logic: Encapsulates the construction process in a builder class.
  3. Flexibility: Allows different configurations or representations of the same object.

Benefits

  1. Clarity: Simplifies the construction of complex objects by breaking it into manageable steps.
  2. Separation of Concerns: Decouples the object construction process from the object itself.
  3. Reusable Code: Enables reuse of the construction process for different object configurations.
  4. Improved Readability: Makes object creation expressive and easier to understand.

Implementation

Scenario: Building a Computer Configuration

1. Product Class

The object to be built.

Code:

public class Computer
{
    public string Processor { get; set; }
    public string RAM { get; set; }
    public string Storage { get; set; }
    public string GraphicsCard { get; set; }

    public override string ToString()
    {
        return $"Processor: {Processor}, RAM: {RAM}, Storage: {Storage}, Graphics Card: {GraphicsCard}";
    }
}

2. Builder Interface

Defines the steps for building the object.

Code:

public interface IComputerBuilder
{
    void SetProcessor(string processor);
    void SetRAM(string ram);
    void SetStorage(string storage);
    void SetGraphicsCard(string graphicsCard);
    Computer GetComputer();
}

3. Concrete Builder

Implements the steps defined in the builder interface.

Code:

public class GamingComputerBuilder : IComputerBuilder
{
    private readonly Computer _computer = new Computer();

    public void SetProcessor(string processor)
    {
        _computer.Processor = processor;
    }

    public void SetRAM(string ram)
    {
        _computer.RAM = ram;
    }

    public void SetStorage(string storage)
    {
        _computer.Storage = storage;
    }

    public void SetGraphicsCard(string graphicsCard)
    {
        _computer.GraphicsCard = graphicsCard;
    }

    public Computer GetComputer()
    {
        return _computer;
    }
}

4. Director

Orchestrates the construction process.

Code:

public class ComputerDirector
{
    private readonly IComputerBuilder _builder;

    public ComputerDirector(IComputerBuilder builder)
    {
        _builder = builder;
    }

    public void BuildGamingComputer()
    {
        _builder.SetProcessor("Intel i9");
        _builder.SetRAM("32GB");
        _builder.SetStorage("2TB SSD");
        _builder.SetGraphicsCard("NVIDIA RTX 4090");
    }
}

5. Client Code

Demonstrates the usage of the builder.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        IComputerBuilder builder = new GamingComputerBuilder();
        ComputerDirector director = new ComputerDirector(builder);

        director.BuildGamingComputer();
        Computer gamingComputer = builder.GetComputer();

        Console.WriteLine(gamingComputer);
    }
}

Output:

Processor: Intel i9, RAM: 32GB, Storage: 2TB SSD, Graphics Card: NVIDIA RTX 4090

Variations

Fluent builder

Uses method chaining to improve readability.

Example:

public class FluentComputerBuilder
{
    private readonly Computer _computer = new Computer();

    public FluentComputerBuilder SetProcessor(string processor)
    {
        _computer.Processor = processor;
        return this;
    }

    public FluentComputerBuilder SetRAM(string ram)
    {
        _computer.RAM = ram;
        return this;
    }

    public FluentComputerBuilder SetStorage(string storage)
    {
        _computer.Storage = storage;
        return this;
    }

    public FluentComputerBuilder SetGraphicsCard(string graphicsCard)
    {
        _computer.GraphicsCard = graphicsCard;
        return this;
    }

    public Computer Build()
    {
        return _computer;
    }
}

Usage:

Computer computer = new FluentComputerBuilder()
    .SetProcessor("Intel i7")
    .SetRAM("16GB")
    .SetStorage("1TB SSD")
    .SetGraphicsCard("NVIDIA RTX 3080")
    .Build();

Console.WriteLine(computer);

Use cases

  1. Complex Object Creation: When creating an object involves multiple steps or configurations.
  2. Multiple Representations: When the same construction process needs to produce different configurations.
  3. Improved Readability: When constructors with many parameters make the code less readable.

Advantages

  1. Encapsulation of Construction Logic: Keeps object construction logic separate from the object itself.
  2. Reusability: Reuse the builder to create different representations of the same object.
  3. Readable Code: Improves code readability with step-by-step construction.

Disadvantages

  1. Increased Complexity: Adds additional classes for the builder and director.
  2. Overhead for Simple Objects: May not be justified for objects with simple construction requirements.


Structural

Introduction



Adapter pattern

What it is?

The Adapter pattern is a structural design pattern that allows incompatible interfaces to work together. It acts as a bridge between two classes or systems, enabling them to communicate without modifying their existing implementations.


The Adapter pattern:

  • Converts the interface of one class into another interface expected by the client.
  • Allows objects with incompatible interfaces to collaborate.
  • Promotes reuse of existing classes without altering their source code.

Key characteristics

  1. Interface Translation: Adapts the interface of a class to match what the client expects.
  2. Decoupling: Decouples the client code from the class with the incompatible interface.
  3. Flexibility: Allows integration of new or legacy code without modification.

Benefits

  1. Reusability: Enables reuse of existing classes without changing their code.
  2. Flexibility: Adapts third-party or legacy classes to work with new systems.
  3. Separation of Concerns: Keeps the adaptation logic separate from the main business logic.

Implementation

Scenario: Integrating a Third-Party Payment System

Suppose your application works with a payment gateway interface, but you need to integrate a third-party payment processor with a different interface.

1. Target Interface

The interface expected by the client.

Code:

public interface IPaymentGateway
{
    void ProcessPayment(string account, double amount);
}

2. Adaptee

The class with the incompatible interface.

Code:

public class ThirdPartyPaymentProcessor
{
    public void MakePayment(string accountNumber, double paymentAmount)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Payment of {paymentAmount} made to account {accountNumber} using third-party processor.");
    }
}

3. Adapter

The class that bridges the gap between the target interface and the adaptee.

Code:

public class PaymentAdapter : IPaymentGateway
{
    private readonly ThirdPartyPaymentProcessor _thirdPartyProcessor;

    public PaymentAdapter(ThirdPartyPaymentProcessor thirdPartyProcessor)
    {
        _thirdPartyProcessor = thirdPartyProcessor;
    }

    public void ProcessPayment(string account, double amount)
    {
        _thirdPartyProcessor.MakePayment(account, amount);
    }
}

4. Client Code

Demonstrates how the adapter enables the integration.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        ThirdPartyPaymentProcessor thirdPartyProcessor = new ThirdPartyPaymentProcessor();
        IPaymentGateway paymentGateway = new PaymentAdapter(thirdPartyProcessor);

        paymentGateway.ProcessPayment("123456", 500.0);
    }
}

Output:

Payment of 500 made to account 123456 using third-party processor.

Types

  1. Class Adapter:

    • Achieved through inheritance.
    • Extends both the target interface and the adaptee.
    • Not commonly used in C# due to the lack of multiple inheritance.

  2. Object Adapter:

    • Achieved through composition (preferred in C#).
    • The adapter contains an instance of the adaptee and translates calls to it.

Use cases

  1. Integrating Legacy Systems: When new code needs to work with legacy systems that have incompatible interfaces.
  2. Third-Party Libraries: When adapting third-party APIs to work with your application.
  3. Interface Compatibility: When multiple classes need to work together but have incompatible interfaces.

Advantages

  1. Promotes Reuse: Allows existing classes to be reused in new contexts.
  2. Decoupling: Decouples the client code from the implementation details of the adaptee.
  3. Improved Flexibility: Facilitates integration with third-party or legacy systems.

Disadvantages

  1. Increased Complexity: Adds an additional layer of abstraction.
  2. Performance Overhead: May introduce a slight performance cost due to the extra indirection.

Examples

  1. .NET Adapters: Adapters are commonly used to bridge interfaces between different libraries or systems in .NET applications.
  2. Database Access: Adapting a legacy database API to work with a modern ORM like Entity Framework.
  3. File Handling: Wrapping different file storage systems to expose a unified interface.


Bridge pattern

What it is?

The Bridge pattern is a structural design pattern that decouples an abstraction from its implementation, allowing them to evolve independently. Unlike the Adapter pattern, which is used to make two incompatible interfaces work together, the Bridge pattern focuses on designing systems to enable flexibility and scalability by separating concerns.


The Bridge pattern:

  • Separates abstraction from implementation.
  • Facilitates independent evolution of abstraction and implementation.
  • Promotes flexibility by allowing runtime binding of abstractions to implementations.

Key characteristics

  1. Decoupled Abstraction and Implementation: The abstraction (interface or abstract class) defines high-level operations, while the implementation defines low-level operations.
  2. Composition Over Inheritance: Uses composition to achieve flexibility instead of inheritance.
  3. Runtime Binding: Enables dynamic assignment of different implementations to abstractions.

Benefits

  1. Flexibility: Abstraction and implementation can evolve independently.
  2. Reusability: Promotes reuse of both abstractions and implementations.
  3. Scalability: Adding new abstractions or implementations is straightforward without affecting existing code.
  4. Improved Maintenance: Clear separation of concerns simplifies understanding and modification.

Components

  1. Abstraction:

    • Defines the high-level interface for the client.
    • Holds a reference to the implementor.

  2. Refined Abstraction:

    • Extends the abstraction to add additional functionality.

  3. Implementor:

    • Defines the interface for the concrete implementations.

  4. Concrete Implementor:

    • Provides the specific implementation of the implementor interface.

Implementation

Scenario: Sending Notifications via Different Channels

1. Abstraction

Defines the interface for sending notifications.

Code:

public abstract class Notification
{
    protected INotificationSender sender;

    public Notification(INotificationSender sender)
    {
        this.sender = sender;
    }

    public abstract void Send(string message);
}

2. Implementor

Defines the interface for notification senders.

Code:

public interface INotificationSender
{
    void SendMessage(string message);
}

3. Concrete Implementors

Provide specific implementations for sending notifications.

Email Notification Sender:

public class EmailSender : INotificationSender
{
    public void SendMessage(string message)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Email sent: {message}");
    }
}

SMS Notification Sender:

public class SmsSender : INotificationSender
{
    public void SendMessage(string message)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"SMS sent: {message}");
    }
}

4. Refined Abstraction

Extends the abstraction for specific types of notifications.

Code:

public class UrgentNotification : Notification
{
    public UrgentNotification(INotificationSender sender) : base(sender) { }

    public override void Send(string message)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Urgent Notification:");
        sender.SendMessage(message);
    }
}

5. Client Code

Demonstrates the usage of the Bridge pattern.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        INotificationSender emailSender = new EmailSender();
        Notification emailNotification = new UrgentNotification(emailSender);
        emailNotification.Send("Server is down!");

        INotificationSender smsSender = new SmsSender();
        Notification smsNotification = new UrgentNotification(smsSender);
        smsNotification.Send("Critical database issue detected!");
    }
}

Output:

Urgent Notification:
Email sent: Server is down!
Urgent Notification:
SMS sent: Critical database issue detected!

Use cases

  1. Independent Evolution: When abstraction and implementation are expected to change independently.
  2. Multiple Implementations: When a class needs to work with multiple implementations of a behavior or functionality.
  3. Decouple High-Level Logic: When you want to decouple high-level logic from platform-specific details.

Comparison: Bridge vs. Adapter

Aspect

Bridge

Adapter

Purpose

Decouples abstraction from implementation

Makes two incompatible interfaces work together

Usage Context

Used for designing systems to evolve independently

Used for integrating legacy or third-party code

Timing

Applied during design time

Applied during integration time

Advantages

  1. Scalability: Adding new abstractions or implementations does not require changes to existing code.
  2. Encapsulation: Hides implementation details from the client.
  3. Promotes Reusability: Both abstractions and implementations can be reused independently.

Disadvantages

  1. Complexity: Introduces additional layers of abstraction, which may increase complexity.
  2. Overhead: For simple systems, the benefits of decoupling may not outweigh the added design overhead.

Examples

  1. UI Frameworks: Decoupling platform-specific rendering logic from high-level UI components.
  2. Device Drivers: Abstracting hardware-specific details from high-level device interfaces.
  3. Messaging Systems: Decoupling message formats from transport protocols.



Composite pattern

What it is?

The Composite pattern is a structural design pattern used to treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly. It allows you to build a tree-like structure of objects where clients can interact with both individual objects and groups of objects in the same way.


The Composite pattern:

  • Composes objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies.
  • Lets clients treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly.
  • Promotes the Open/Closed Principle, making it easy to add new components without modifying existing code.

Key characteristics

  1. Uniform Interface: Provides a common interface for both leaf nodes (individual objects) and composite nodes (groups of objects).
  2. Recursive Composition: Composite nodes can contain both leaf nodes and other composite nodes.
  3. Client Transparency: The client interacts with objects in the tree without needing to distinguish between leaf and composite nodes.

Benefits

  1. Simplifies Client Code: Treats individual and composite objects uniformly.
  2. Extensibility: Easy to add new component types without modifying existing code.
  3. Flexibility: Allows you to build complex structures dynamically.
  4. Reusability: Components can be reused in multiple compositions.

Implementation

Scenario: File System Hierarchy

Imagine a file system where files and directories are treated uniformly.

1. Component Interface

Defines the common interface for leaf and composite objects.

Code:

public interface IFileSystemComponent
{
    void Display(string indent = "");
}

2. Leaf Class

Represents individual objects in the composition.

Code:

public class File : IFileSystemComponent
{
    private readonly string _name;

    public File(string name)
    {
        _name = name;
    }

    public void Display(string indent = "")
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{indent}- {_name}");
    }
}

3. Composite Class

Represents a group of objects. It can contain both leaf nodes and other composite nodes.

Code:

public class Directory : IFileSystemComponent
{
    private readonly string _name;
    private readonly List<IFileSystemComponent> _components = new();

    public Directory(string name)
    {
        _name = name;
    }

    public void Add(IFileSystemComponent component)
    {
        _components.Add(component);
    }

    public void Remove(IFileSystemComponent component)
    {
        _components.Remove(component);
    }

    public void Display(string indent = "")
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{indent}+ {_name}");
        foreach (var component in _components)
        {
            component.Display(indent + "  ");
        }
    }
}

4. Client Code

Demonstrates how to use the Composite pattern.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        // Create leaf nodesvar file1 = new File("File1.txt");
        var file2 = new File("File2.txt");
        var file3 = new File("File3.txt");

        // Create composite nodesvar folder1 = new Directory("Folder1");
        var folder2 = new Directory("Folder2");

        // Build the hierarchy
        folder1.Add(file1);
        folder1.Add(file2);

        folder2.Add(file3);
        folder2.Add(folder1);

        // Display the hierarchy
        folder2.Display();
    }
}

Output

+ Folder2
  - File3.txt
  + Folder1
    - File1.txt
    - File2.txt

Use cases

  1. Hierarchical Structures: When objects are naturally organized in a tree structure, such as file systems, menus, or organizational charts.
  2. Uniform Treatment: When individual objects and compositions need to be treated the same way.
  3. Dynamic Structure: When structures need to be built, modified, or traversed dynamically at runtime.

Advantages

  1. Simplifies Client Code: No need for client code to distinguish between individual and composite objects.
  2. Promotes Consistency: Ensures that all components adhere to the same interface.
  3. Encapsulation: Encapsulates complex tree structures, making them easier to manage.
  4. Extensibility: Adding new component types does not require modifying existing code.

Disadvantages

  1. Complexity: May introduce unnecessary complexity for simple structures.
  2. Overhead: Managing large trees can introduce performance and memory overhead.
  3. Encapsulation Leakage: Clients may need to understand the differences between leaf and composite nodes in certain scenarios.

Examples

  1. UI Component Hierarchies: Building user interfaces with nested components (e.g., panels, buttons, text fields).
  2. File Systems: Managing files and directories in a hierarchical structure.
  3. Menus: Representing menus and submenus in a uniform structure.

Best practices

  1. Define a Clear Interface: Ensure all components (leaf and composite) adhere to the same interface.
  2. Encapsulate Tree Management: Keep tree management logic (e.g., adding/removing components) within the composite class.
  3. Optimize for Large Trees: Use caching or lazy-loading strategies for large and complex tree structures.


Decorator pattern

What it is?

The Decorator pattern is a structural design pattern that allows you to dynamically add behavior or responsibilities to an object at runtime without modifying its structure. It provides a flexible alternative to subclassing for extending functionality.


The Decorator pattern:

  • Wraps an object to extend its behavior without altering its code.
  • Allows behaviors to be added or removed dynamically at runtime.
  • Promotes the Open/Closed Principle by enabling extensions without modifying existing code.

Key characteristics

  1. Composition Over Inheritance: Uses composition to extend functionality rather than inheritance.
  2. Dynamic Behavior: Allows behavior to be added or removed at runtime.
  3. Flexible Decoration: Multiple decorators can be combined to add layered behavior.

Benefits

  1. Flexibility: Adds new functionality dynamically without modifying existing code.
  2. Reusability: Decorators can be reused independently to extend behavior.
  3. Scalability: Multiple decorators can be stacked for complex extensions.
  4. Adherence to SOLID Principles: Promotes the Open/Closed Principle by extending behavior without modification.

Implementation

Scenario: Adding Features to a Notification System

1. Component Interface

Defines the common interface for both core objects and decorators.

Code:

public interface INotifier
{
    void Send(string message);
}

2. Concrete Component

The base object that can be extended.

Code:

public class EmailNotifier : INotifier
{
    public void Send(string message)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Sending Email: {message}");
    }
}

3. Base Decorator

Wraps the component and provides a base for additional decorators.

Code:

public abstract class NotifierDecorator : INotifier
{
    protected readonly INotifier _notifier;

    protected NotifierDecorator(INotifier notifier)
    {
        _notifier = notifier;
    }

    public virtual void Send(string message)
    {
        _notifier.Send(message);
    }
}

4. Concrete Decorators

Add new behavior to the base component.

SMS Notification Decorator:

public class SmsNotifier : NotifierDecorator
{
    public SmsNotifier(INotifier notifier) : base(notifier) { }

    public override void Send(string message)
    {
        base.Send(message);
        Console.WriteLine($"Sending SMS: {message}");
    }
}

Slack Notification Decorator:

public class SlackNotifier : NotifierDecorator
{
    public SlackNotifier(INotifier notifier) : base(notifier) { }

    public override void Send(string message)
    {
        base.Send(message);
        Console.WriteLine($"Sending Slack message: {message}");
    }
}

5. Client Code

Demonstrates dynamic addition of behaviors.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        // Base notifier
        INotifier notifier = new EmailNotifier();

        // Add SMS notification
        notifier = new SmsNotifier(notifier);

        // Add Slack notification
        notifier = new SlackNotifier(notifier);

        // Send notifications
        notifier.Send("Server is down!");
    }
}

Output

Sending Email: Server is down!
Sending SMS: Server is down!
Sending Slack message: Server is down!

Use cases

  1. Dynamic Behavior: When you need to add behavior dynamically to an object at runtime.
  2. Avoiding Subclass Explosion: When inheritance would lead to a large number of subclasses to represent all combinations of behaviors.
  3. Reusing Extensions: When you want to reuse the same extensions across different objects.

Advantages

  1. Extensibility: Allows you to extend functionality without modifying existing classes.
  2. Layered Behavior: Supports combining multiple behaviors dynamically.
  3. Promotes Single Responsibility: Each decorator focuses on a specific responsibility.

Disadvantages

  1. Complexity: Can increase complexity with multiple layers of decorators.
  2. Debugging Challenges: Debugging can be harder due to the dynamic composition of objects.

Comparison with related patterns

Decorator

Adapter

Composite

Adds new behavior dynamically

Converts one interface into another

Relationship

Bridges two incompatible interfaces

Examples

  1. Stream Classes in .NET: Classes like BufferedStream, CryptoStream, and DeflateStream are decorators for base streams.
  2. UI Frameworks: Wrapping UI components to add behaviors like scrolling, borders, or shadows.
  3. Logging Systems: Adding additional logging behaviors dynamically (e.g., logging to a file, console, or external service).


Facade pattern

What it is?

The Facade pattern is a structural design pattern that provides a simplified, unified interface to a set of complex subsystems. It hides the complexities of the underlying subsystems and provides a higher-level abstraction to the client.


The Facade pattern:

  • Simplifies access to a complex system by providing a unified interface.
  • Reduces dependencies between clients and subsystems.
  • Promotes loose coupling by shielding clients from the implementation details of subsystems.

Key characteristics

  1. Simplified Interface: Provides an easy-to-use interface for complex subsystems.
  2. Encapsulation: Hides the details of subsystem implementations from the client.
  3. Decoupling: Minimizes direct dependencies between clients and subsystems.

Benefits

  1. Improved Usability: Simplifies client interaction with complex systems.
  2. Loose Coupling: Decouples clients from subsystem implementations.
  3. Single Entry Point: Provides a unified entry point to the subsystem.
  4. Encapsulation of Complexity: Shields clients from the intricacies of the subsystems.

Implementation

Scenario: Home Theater System

A home theater system consists of multiple subsystems like a projector, sound system, and Blu-ray player. The Facade provides a simple interface to operate all subsystems.

1. Subsystems

The individual subsystems with their own logic.

Projector:

public class Projector
{
    public void TurnOn()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Projector is On.");
    }

    public void TurnOff()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Projector is Off.");
    }
}

Sound System:

public class SoundSystem
{
    public void TurnOn()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Sound System is On.");
    }

    public void TurnOff()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Sound System is Off.");
    }
}

Blu-ray Player:

public class BluRayPlayer
{
    public void TurnOn()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Blu-ray Player is On.");
    }

    public void PlayMovie(string movie)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Playing movie: {movie}");
    }

    public void TurnOff()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Blu-ray Player is Off.");
    }
}

2. Facade

Provides a simplified interface for the subsystems.

Code:

public class HomeTheaterFacade
{
    private readonly Projector _projector;
    private readonly SoundSystem _soundSystem;
    private readonly BluRayPlayer _bluRayPlayer;

    public HomeTheaterFacade(Projector projector, SoundSystem soundSystem, BluRayPlayer bluRayPlayer)
    {
        _projector = projector;
        _soundSystem = soundSystem;
        _bluRayPlayer = bluRayPlayer;
    }

    public void StartMovie(string movie)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Setting up the home theater...");
        _projector.TurnOn();
        _soundSystem.TurnOn();
        _bluRayPlayer.TurnOn();
        _bluRayPlayer.PlayMovie(movie);
        Console.WriteLine("Enjoy your movie!");
    }

    public void EndMovie()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Shutting down the home theater...");
        _bluRayPlayer.TurnOff();
        _soundSystem.TurnOff();
        _projector.TurnOff();
        Console.WriteLine("Goodbye!");
    }
}

3. Client Code

Demonstrates the use of the Facade.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        // Create subsystemsvar projector = new Projector();
        var soundSystem = new SoundSystem();
        var bluRayPlayer = new BluRayPlayer();

        // Create facadevar homeTheater = new HomeTheaterFacade(projector, soundSystem, bluRayPlayer);

        // Use facade
        homeTheater.StartMovie("Inception");
        Console.WriteLine();
        homeTheater.EndMovie();
    }
}

Output

Setting up the home theater...
Projector is On.
Sound System is On.
Blu-ray Player is On.
Playing movie: Inception
Enjoy your movie!

Shutting down the home theater...
Blu-ray Player is Off.
Sound System is Off.
Projector is Off.
Goodbye!

Use cases

  1. Simplifying Complex Subsystems: When a system has multiple subsystems with intricate interfaces.
  2. Decoupling Clients from Subsystems: When you want to minimize dependencies between clients and subsystems.
  3. Single Entry Point: When you need a unified interface to manage a system.

Advantages

  1. Encapsulation: Hides subsystem complexities from clients.
  2. Improved Usability: Simplifies interaction with complex systems.
  3. Loose Coupling: Reduces dependency between clients and subsystems.
  4. Extensibility: Allows subsystems to evolve independently of client code.

Disadvantages

  1. Over-Simplification: May limit access to specific features of subsystems.
  2. Single Point of Failure: The facade becomes a bottleneck if poorly implemented.

  2. Database Access: Simplifying interaction with databases through an abstraction layer.
  3. Web APIs: Providing a single API endpoint to manage multiple backend services.


Flyweight pattern

What it is?

The Flyweight pattern is a structural design pattern that focuses on minimizing memory usage by sharing as much data as possible with similar objects. It is particularly useful when working with a large number of similar objects that share common data.


The Flyweight pattern:

  • Reduces memory consumption by sharing common parts of object state.

  • Divides object state into intrinsic and extrinsic data:

    • Intrinsic State: Shared between multiple objects and stored in the Flyweight.
    • Extrinsic State: Unique to each object and passed by the client when needed.
  • Optimizes memory and improves performance in systems with many similar objects.

Key characteristics

  1. Shared State: Intrinsic data is shared between multiple objects.
  2. Minimized Memory Usage: Reduces memory overhead by reusing shared objects.
  3. Decoupling: Separates shared (intrinsic) and non-shared (extrinsic) data.

Benefits

  1. Memory Efficiency: Reduces memory consumption by sharing intrinsic data.
  2. Improved Performance: Optimizes resource usage for large collections of objects.
  3. Scalability: Handles large numbers of objects effectively.

Implementation

Scenario: Formatting Characters in a Document**

1. Flyweight Interface

Defines the interface for shared objects.

Code:

public interface ICharacter
{
    void Display(int fontSize);
}

2. Concrete Flyweight

Implements the Flyweight interface and contains shared data.

Code:

public class Character : ICharacter
{
    private readonly char _symbol; // Intrinsic state (shared)public Character(char symbol)
    {
        _symbol = symbol;
    }

    public void Display(int fontSize) // Extrinsic state (passed by client)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Character: {_symbol}, Font Size: {fontSize}");
    }
}

3. Flyweight Factory

Manages Flyweight objects and ensures they are shared.

Code:

public class CharacterFactory
{
    private readonly Dictionary<char, ICharacter> _characters = new();

    public ICharacter GetCharacter(char symbol)
    {
        if (!_characters.ContainsKey(symbol))
        {
            _characters[symbol] = new Character(symbol);
        }
        return _characters[symbol];
    }
}

4. Client Code

Uses Flyweight objects and passes extrinsic state.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        var factory = new CharacterFactory();

        string document = "ABBA";

        int[] fontSizes = { 12, 14, 16, 12 };

        for (int i = 0; i < document.Length; i++)
        {
            char symbol = document[i];
            int fontSize = fontSizes[i];

            ICharacter character = factory.GetCharacter(symbol);
            character.Display(fontSize);
        }
    }
}

Output

Character: A, Font Size: 12
Character: B, Font Size: 14
Character: B, Font Size: 16
Character: A, Font Size: 12

How it works

  1. The Flyweight Factory manages and reuses Flyweight objects (e.g., Character objects for each unique letter).
  2. The Client provides extrinsic data (e.g., font size) at runtime.
  3. Flyweight Objects combine shared intrinsic state with unique extrinsic state to fulfill client requests.

Use cases

  1. High Volume of Similar Objects: When a system requires a large number of objects with shared data.
  2. Memory Optimization: When object creation and memory usage need to be minimized.
  3. Shared State: When objects share a significant portion of their state.

Advantages

  1. Memory Efficiency: Reduces memory usage by sharing intrinsic data.
  2. Improved Performance: Optimizes the creation and management of similar objects.
  3. Scalability: Handles large-scale systems effectively.

Disadvantages

  1. Complexity: Adds complexity by separating intrinsic and extrinsic data.
  2. Runtime State Management: Requires the client to manage extrinsic data explicitly.
  3. Applicability: Not suitable for systems where objects have little or no shared state.

Examples

  1. Text Editors: Sharing character glyphs in a document while storing formatting as extrinsic state.
  2. Game Development: Reusing sprites or models for characters and objects with unique positions or states.
  3. Caching Systems: Sharing cache entries for data with common attributes.

Comparison with related patterns

Best practices

  1. Separate Intrinsic and Extrinsic Data: Clearly identify shared and unique data.
  2. Use Flyweight Factory: Centralize the creation and reuse of Flyweight objects.
  3. Avoid Overuse: Use only when memory optimization justifies the added complexity.


Proxy pattern

What it is?

The Proxy pattern is a structural design pattern that provides a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it. A proxy can add additional behavior, such as lazy initialization, access control, or logging, without modifying the original object's code.


The Proxy pattern:

  • Acts as an intermediary between the client and the real object.
  • Controls access to the real object, adding additional behavior or logic.
  • Can be used to defer the creation or initialization of resource-intensive objects.

Key characteristics

  1. Intermediary: The proxy sits between the client and the real object.
  2. Control Access: The proxy can implement access control, logging, caching, or lazy initialization.
  3. Same Interface: The proxy and the real object share the same interface, making them interchangeable.

Benefits

  1. Controlled Access: Restricts or manages access to the real object.
  2. Lazy Initialization: Defers the creation of resource-intensive objects until they are needed.
  3. Additional Behavior: Adds logging, caching, or other functionality without modifying the real object.
  4. Decoupling: Decouples the client from the details of accessing the real object.

Implementation

Scenario: Accessing a Resource-Intensive Image

1. Subject Interface

Defines the common interface for the real object and its proxy.

Code:

public interface IImage
{
    void Display();
}

2. Real Subject

Implements the interface and contains the actual logic.

Code:

public class RealImage : IImage
{
    private readonly string _fileName;

    public RealImage(string fileName)
    {
        _fileName = fileName;
        LoadFromDisk();
    }

    private void LoadFromDisk()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Loading {_fileName} from disk...");
    }

    public void Display()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Displaying {_fileName}");
    }
}

3. Proxy

Controls access to the real object and adds behavior (e.g., lazy initialization).

Code:

public class ProxyImage : IImage
{
    private RealImage _realImage;
    private readonly string _fileName;

    public ProxyImage(string fileName)
    {
        _fileName = fileName;
    }

    public void Display()
    {
        if (_realImage == null)
        {
            _realImage = new RealImage(_fileName);
        }
        _realImage.Display();
    }
}

4. Client Code

Uses the proxy to access the real object.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        IImage image = new ProxyImage("photo.jpg");

        // Image is not loaded yet
        Console.WriteLine("Image created, but not loaded.");

        // Load and display the image
        image.Display();

        // Display again without loading
        image.Display();
    }
}

Output

Image created, but not loaded.
Loading photo.jpg from disk...
Displaying photo.jpg
Displaying photo.jpg

Types

  1. Virtual Proxy: Defers object creation or initialization until necessary.
  2. Protection Proxy: Controls access to the real object, enforcing permissions.
  3. Remote Proxy: Represents an object that resides in a different address space (e.g., a remote server).
  4. Caching Proxy: Adds caching behavior to reduce expensive operations.
  5. Smart Proxy: Adds additional behavior, such as reference counting or logging.

Use cases

  1. Resource-Intensive Objects: When creating or loading an object is costly, and it should be deferred until needed.
  2. Access Control: When access to the real object must be restricted or controlled.
  3. Additional Behavior: When you need to add logging, caching, or similar behavior without modifying the real object.

Advantages

  1. Improved Performance: Delays costly operations until necessary.
  2. Encapsulation: Encapsulates additional behavior, such as logging or caching, without modifying the real object.
  3. Controlled Access: Provides a single point of control for access to the real object.
  4. Decoupling: Decouples the client from the real object's lifecycle and implementation details.

Disadvantages

  1. Increased Complexity: Adds additional layers of abstraction.
  2. Overhead: Can introduce performance overhead due to the proxy's behavior.
  3. Dependency on Proxy: Clients become dependent on the proxy, which may introduce maintenance challenges.

  1. Database Connections: Proxies managing database connections to handle lazy initialization and access control.
  2. Remote Access: Remote proxies for accessing objects on a remote server.

Behavioral

Introduction



Chain of responsibility pattern

What it is?

The Chain of Responsibility pattern is a behavioral design pattern that allows multiple objects to process a request without coupling the sender to the receiver. The pattern creates a chain of handlers, where each handler decides whether to process the request or pass it to the next handler in the chain.


The Chain of Responsibility pattern:

  • Delegates requests along a chain of handlers.
  • Allows each handler to either process the request or pass it to the next handler.
  • Decouples the sender and receiver of a request.

Key characteristics

  1. Dynamic Chain: Handlers can be dynamically added, removed, or reordered in the chain.
  2. Decoupling: The sender does not need to know which handler will process the request.
  3. Flexible Responsibility: Responsibility can be distributed across multiple handlers.

Benefits

  1. Decoupling: Reduces tight coupling between sender and receivers.
  2. Flexibility: Allows runtime modification of the chain.
  3. Single Responsibility: Each handler focuses on a specific task or condition.
  4. Scalability: New handlers can be added without modifying existing code.

Implementation

Scenario: Processing User Requests with Multiple Validation Steps

1. Handler Interface

Defines the common interface for all handlers in the chain.

Code:

public interface IHandler
{
    void SetNext(IHandler next);
    void HandleRequest(string request);
}

2. Abstract Handler

Provides a base implementation for chaining handlers.

Code:

public abstract class Handler : IHandler
{
    private IHandler _nextHandler;

    public void SetNext(IHandler next)
    {
        _nextHandler = next;
    }

    public virtual void HandleRequest(string request)
    {
        if (_nextHandler != null)
        {
            _nextHandler.HandleRequest(request);
        }
    }
}

3. Concrete Handlers

Implement specific logic for handling requests.

Authentication Handler:

public class AuthenticationHandler : Handler
{
    public override void HandleRequest(string request)
    {
        if (request.Contains("Auth"))
        {
            Console.WriteLine("Authentication Successful.");
        }
        else
        {
            Console.WriteLine("Authentication Failed.");
        }
        base.HandleRequest(request);
    }
}

Authorization Handler:

public class AuthorizationHandler : Handler
{
    public override void HandleRequest(string request)
    {
        if (request.Contains("Admin"))
        {
            Console.WriteLine("Authorization Granted.");
        }
        else
        {
            Console.WriteLine("Authorization Denied.");
        }
        base.HandleRequest(request);
    }
}

Logging Handler:

public class LoggingHandler : Handler
{
    public override void HandleRequest(string request)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Logging Request: {request}");
        base.HandleRequest(request);
    }
}

4. Client Code

Demonstrates how to use the chain of handlers.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        // Create handlersvar authHandler = new AuthenticationHandler();
        var authorizationHandler = new AuthorizationHandler();
        var loggingHandler = new LoggingHandler();

        // Build the chain
        authHandler.SetNext(authorizationHandler);
        authorizationHandler.SetNext(loggingHandler);

        // Send a request
        Console.WriteLine("Processing Request 1:");
        authHandler.HandleRequest("Auth Admin");

        Console.WriteLine();

        Console.WriteLine("Processing Request 2:");
        authHandler.HandleRequest("Guest");
    }
}

Output

Processing Request 1:
Authentication Successful.
Authorization Granted.
Logging Request: Auth Admin.

Processing Request 2:
Authentication Failed.
Authorization Denied.
Logging Request: Guest.

How it works

  1. Chain Construction: Handlers are linked together in a sequence using the SetNext method.
  2. Request Processing: A request is passed to the first handler. Each handler can process the request or forward it to the next handler.
  3. Dynamic Extension: New handlers can be added to the chain without altering existing handlers.

Use cases

  1. Multiple Processors: When a request can be handled by more than one handler.
  2. Dynamic Chains: When the order or number of handlers needs to be dynamic.
  3. Decoupling Sender and Receiver: When the sender should not know which handler will process the request.

Advantages

  1. Reduced Coupling: Decouples sender and receiver by allowing multiple handlers.
  2. Runtime Flexibility: Handlers can be added, removed, or reordered dynamically.
  3. Improved Maintenance: Each handler focuses on a specific responsibility.

Disadvantages

  1. No Guarantee of Handling: A request might not be handled if no handler is responsible.
  2. Debugging Challenges: Tracing the flow of a request through multiple handlers can be complex.
  3. Performance Overhead: The request may pass through many handlers before being processed.

Command pattern

What it is?

The Command pattern is a behavioral design pattern that encapsulates a request as an object, allowing you to parameterize objects with operations, delay execution, or queue operations. It decouples the sender of a request from its receiver, promoting flexibility and extensibility.


The Command pattern:

  • Encapsulates requests as objects, known as commands.
  • Decouples the sender of the request (invoker) from the object that executes it (receiver).
  • Supports undo/redo functionality, queuing requests, and logging operations.

Key characteristics

  1. Encapsulation: Encapsulates a request into a command object.
  2. Decoupling: Decouples the invoker and the receiver of the request.
  3. Reusability: Commands can be reused and composed in different ways.

Benefits

  1. Undo/Redo Functionality: Supports reversing executed commands.
  2. Flexibility: Allows requests to be queued, logged, or delayed.
  3. Extensibility: Adding new commands does not affect existing code.
  4. Decoupling: Reduces dependencies between the sender and receiver.

Implementation

Scenario: Remote Control System for Devices

A remote control sends commands to different devices (e.g., TV, Sound System). Commands encapsulate the actions and allow for flexible execution.

1. Command Interface

Defines the common interface for all commands.

Code:

public interface ICommand
{
    void Execute();
    void Undo();
}

2. Receiver

Performs the actual operations.

Code:

public class Television
{
    public void TurnOn()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("The TV is On.");
    }

    public void TurnOff()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("The TV is Off.");
    }
}

3. Concrete Commands

Encapsulate requests and delegate execution to the receiver.

Turn On Command:

public class TurnOnCommand : ICommand
{
    private readonly Television _tv;

    public TurnOnCommand(Television tv)
    {
        _tv = tv;
    }

    public void Execute()
    {
        _tv.TurnOn();
    }

    public void Undo()
    {
        _tv.TurnOff();
    }
}

Turn Off Command:

public class TurnOffCommand : ICommand
{
    private readonly Television _tv;

    public TurnOffCommand(Television tv)
    {
        _tv = tv;
    }

    public void Execute()
    {
        _tv.TurnOff();
    }

    public void Undo()
    {
        _tv.TurnOn();
    }
}

4. Invoker

Holds commands and triggers their execution.

Code:

public class RemoteControl
{
    private ICommand _command;

    public void SetCommand(ICommand command)
    {
        _command = command;
    }

    public void PressButton()
    {
        _command.Execute();
    }

    public void PressUndo()
    {
        _command.Undo();
    }
}

5. Client Code

Uses the invoker to execute commands.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        // Create receivervar tv = new Television();

        // Create commandsvar turnOn = new TurnOnCommand(tv);
        var turnOff = new TurnOffCommand(tv);

        // Create invokervar remote = new RemoteControl();

        // Execute commands
        remote.SetCommand(turnOn);
        remote.PressButton(); // The TV is On.

        remote.PressUndo(); // The TV is Off.

        remote.SetCommand(turnOff);
        remote.PressButton(); // The TV is Off.
    }
}

Output

plaintext
Copy code
The TV is On.
The TV is Off.
The TV is Off.

How it works

  1. Command Objects: Encapsulate requests and delegate execution to the appropriate receiver.
  2. Invoker: Holds references to commands and triggers their execution.
  3. Receiver: Performs the actual operations requested by the commands.

Use cases

  1. Encapsulating Requests: When requests need to be represented as objects.
  2. Undo/Redo Functionality: When actions need to be reversible.
  3. Queuing or Logging: When requests need to be queued or logged for later execution.
  4. Parameterizing Objects: When objects should be parameterized with operations.

Advantages

  1. Extensibility: Adding new commands is straightforward without modifying existing code.
  2. Undo/Redo Support: Easily supports reversing executed commands.
  3. Flexibility: Commands can be combined or reused in different contexts.
  4. Decoupling: Reduces tight coupling between the sender and receiver.

Disadvantages

  1. Increased Complexity: Adds additional classes and objects for each command.
  2. Memory Overhead: Storing commands for undo/redo operations can increase memory usage.

  2. Task Queues: Queuing operations for execution at a later time.
  3. Undo/Redo Systems: Storing commands for reversing or reapplying actions.


Interpreter pattern

What it is?

The Interpreter pattern is a behavioral design pattern that defines a way to evaluate or interpret sentences in a specific language. The pattern implements a domain-specific language (DSL) by representing each grammar rule as a class and building a syntax tree to interpret or execute commands.


The Interpreter pattern:

  • Provides a way to evaluate expressions or interpret a specific language.
  • Maps a grammar to a class hierarchy, where each rule is represented by a class.
  • Constructs an abstract syntax tree to evaluate expressions or execute commands.

Key characteristics

  1. Grammar Representation: Each grammar rule is encapsulated in a separate class.
  2. Composability: Complex expressions are composed of simpler expressions.
  3. Extensibility: New rules or expressions can be added by creating new classes.

Benefits

  1. Domain-Specific Languages: Enables implementation of a DSL for specific tasks.
  2. Flexibility: Grammar rules can be easily added or modified.
  3. Separation of Concerns: Decouples grammar rules from the logic that uses them.

Implementation

Scenario: Parsing and Evaluating Mathematical Expressions

1. Abstract Expression

Defines the common interface for all expressions.

Code:

public interface IExpression
{
    int Interpret();
}

2. Terminal Expressions

Represents leaf nodes in the abstract syntax tree (e.g., numbers).

Code:

public class Number : IExpression
{
    private readonly int _value;

    public Number(int value)
    {
        _value = value;
    }

    public int Interpret()
    {
        return _value;
    }
}

3. Non-Terminal Expressions

Represents operations (e.g., addition, subtraction).

Addition Expression:

public class Add : IExpression
{
    private readonly IExpression _left;
    private readonly IExpression _right;

    public Add(IExpression left, IExpression right)
    {
        _left = left;
        _right = right;
    }

    public int Interpret()
    {
        return _left.Interpret() + _right.Interpret();
    }
}

Subtraction Expression:

public class Subtract : IExpression
{
    private readonly IExpression _left;
    private readonly IExpression _right;

    public Subtract(IExpression left, IExpression right)
    {
        _left = left;
        _right = right;
    }

    public int Interpret()
    {
        return _left.Interpret() - _right.Interpret();
    }
}

4. Client Code

Constructs the syntax tree and interprets the expression.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        // Build the expression: (5 + 3) - (2 + 1)
        IExpression five = new Number(5);
        IExpression three = new Number(3);
        IExpression two = new Number(2);
        IExpression one = new Number(1);

        IExpression addition1 = new Add(five, three); // (5 + 3)
        IExpression addition2 = new Add(two, one);   // (2 + 1)

        IExpression expression = new Subtract(addition1, addition2); // (5 + 3) - (2 + 1)

        Console.WriteLine($"Result: {expression.Interpret()}");
    }
}

Output

Result: 5

How it works

  1. Expression Tree: An abstract syntax tree is built, where terminal and non-terminal expressions represent grammar rules.
  2. Evaluation: The Interpret method is called recursively on each node of the syntax tree to compute the result.

Use cases

  1. Domain-Specific Languages: When implementing a language for a specific domain (e.g., math expressions, configuration files).
  2. Complex Parsing Logic: When parsing and evaluating expressions require recursive rules.
  3. Dynamic Rule Evaluation: When grammar rules or expressions might change over time.

Advantages

  1. Modularity: Each grammar rule is encapsulated in a separate class.
  2. Extensibility: New grammar rules can be added by creating new classes.
  3. Readable Code: Represents complex expressions in a structured and understandable way.

Disadvantages

  1. Performance Overhead: Large syntax trees can lead to performance issues.
  2. Complexity: Managing a large number of grammar rules can be cumbersome.
  3. Limited Scalability: May not be suitable for complex or high-performance languages.

Examples

  1. Math Expression Evaluators: Parsing and evaluating mathematical expressions.
  2. Query Languages: Implementing custom query languages for filtering or searching.
  3. Configuration Parsers: Reading and interpreting configuration files or scripts.

Mediator pattern

What it is?

The Mediator pattern is a behavioral design pattern that facilitates communication between objects by encapsulating how they interact. Instead of objects communicating directly with each other, they send messages through a central mediator object. This promotes loose coupling and simplifies maintenance.


The Mediator pattern:

  • Centralizes communication between objects (colleagues) via a mediator.
  • Reduces dependencies between objects by decoupling their interactions.
  • Simplifies complex systems where multiple objects interact frequently.

Key characteristics

  1. Centralized Communication: A single mediator handles all communication between objects.
  2. Loose Coupling: Objects interact only with the mediator, not directly with each other.
  3. Simplified Collaboration: Reduces the number of direct dependencies between objects.

Benefits

  1. Reduced Coupling: Promotes loose coupling between components, making the system more maintainable.
  2. Simplified Communication: Centralizes interaction logic, reducing complexity.
  3. Improved Flexibility: Allows easy addition or modification of components without affecting others.
  4. Enhanced Reusability: Mediator logic can be reused or extended without altering individual components.

Implementation

Scenario: Chat Room

A chat room facilitates communication between users without them knowing about each other.

1. Mediator Interface

Defines the contract for the mediator.

Code:

public interface IChatRoomMediator
{
    void SendMessage(string message, User user);
    void RegisterUser(User user);
}

2. Concrete Mediator

Implements the mediator interface and manages communication.

Code:

public class ChatRoom : IChatRoomMediator
{
    private readonly Dictionary<string, User> _users = new();

    public void RegisterUser(User user)
    {
        if (!_users.ContainsKey(user.Name))
        {
            _users[user.Name] = user;
        }
    }

    public void SendMessage(string message, User sender)
    {
        foreach (var user in _users.Values)
        {
            if (user != sender)
            {
                user.Receive(message, sender.Name);
            }
        }
    }
}

3. Colleague Class

Represents the objects that interact via the mediator.

Code:

public class User
{
    private readonly IChatRoomMediator _chatRoom;
    public string Name { get; }

    public User(string name, IChatRoomMediator chatRoom)
    {
        Name = name;
        _chatRoom = chatRoom;
        _chatRoom.RegisterUser(this);
    }

    public void Send(string message)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{Name} sends: {message}");
        _chatRoom.SendMessage(message, this);
    }

    public void Receive(string message, string senderName)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{Name} receives: {message} from {senderName}");
    }
}

4. Client Code

Uses the mediator to manage communication.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        var chatRoom = new ChatRoom();

        var user1 = new User("Alice", chatRoom);
        var user2 = new User("Bob", chatRoom);
        var user3 = new User("Charlie", chatRoom);

        user1.Send("Hello, everyone!");
        user2.Send("Hi Alice!");
        user3.Send("Hey Bob and Alice!");
    }
}

Output

Alice sends: Hello, everyone!
Bob receives: Hello, everyone! from Alice
Charlie receives: Hello, everyone! from Alice

Bob sends: Hi Alice!
Alice receives: Hi Alice! from Bob
Charlie receives: Hi Alice! from Bob

Charlie sends: Hey Bob and Alice!
Alice receives: Hey Bob and Alice! from Charlie
Bob receives: Hey Bob and Alice! from Charlie

How it works

  1. Centralized Communication: Users communicate through the chat room (mediator), not directly with each other.
  2. Decoupling: Each user interacts only with the chat room, reducing dependencies.
  3. Dynamic Management: The chat room manages the addition or removal of users dynamically.

Use cases

  1. Complex Object Interactions:

    • When multiple objects need to communicate frequently and directly.

  2. Loose Coupling:

    • When you want to reduce dependencies between components.

  3. Centralized Logic:

    • When interaction logic should be encapsulated in a single location.

Advantages

  1. Reduced Coupling: Decouples objects, making the system more maintainable.
  2. Improved Modularity: Interaction logic is centralized, simplifying code.
  3. Flexibility: Adding or modifying components becomes easier.
  4. Enhanced Reusability: Components can be reused independently of each other.

Disadvantages

  1. Mediator Complexity: The mediator can become a bottleneck or overly complex as it grows.
  2. Performance Overhead: Centralized communication can introduce delays in high-performance systems.
  3. Single Point of Failure: If the mediator fails, the entire system might be affected.

  2. UI Frameworks: Dialog boxes or mediators managing communication between UI components.
  3. Event Dispatchers: Event systems managing interaction between objects in an application.


Memento pattern

What it is?

The Memento pattern is a behavioral design pattern that provides a way to capture and restore an object's state without exposing its internal details. It is commonly used to implement undo/redo functionality in applications.


The Memento pattern:

  • Encapsulates the internal state of an object in a separate memento object.
  • Provides a mechanism for saving and restoring the object's state without violating encapsulation.
  • Separates the object’s state management (originator) from the state storage (caretaker).

Key components

  1. Originator: The object whose state needs to be saved and restored.
  2. Memento: Stores the internal state of the originator.
  3. Caretaker: Manages the memento, often keeping a history of states for undo/redo purposes.

Benefits

  1. Encapsulation: Keeps the originator's state private while allowing it to be saved and restored.
  2. Undo/Redo Functionality: Simplifies the implementation of undo/redo features in applications.
  3. State Management: Allows object state to be managed independently from its primary behavior.

Implementation

Scenario: Text Editor Undo/Redo

1. Originator

The object whose state is captured and restored.

Code:

public class TextEditor
{
    public string Content { get; set; }

    public Memento Save()
    {
        return new Memento(Content);
    }

    public void Restore(Memento memento)
    {
        Content = memento.Content;
    }
}

2. Memento

Stores the state of the originator.

Code:

public class Memento
{
    public string Content { get; }

    public Memento(string content)
    {
        Content = content;
    }
}

3. Caretaker

Manages the mementos, allowing undo and redo functionality.

Code:

public class Caretaker
{
    private readonly Stack<Memento> _undoStack = new();
    private readonly Stack<Memento> _redoStack = new();

    public void Save(Memento memento)
    {
        _undoStack.Push(memento);
        _redoStack.Clear(); // Clear redo stack after a new save
    }

    public Memento Undo()
    {
        if (_undoStack.Count > 0)
        {
            var memento = _undoStack.Pop();
            _redoStack.Push(memento);
            return memento;
        }
        return null;
    }

    public Memento Redo()
    {
        if (_redoStack.Count > 0)
        {
            var memento = _redoStack.Pop();
            _undoStack.Push(memento);
            return memento;
        }
        return null;
    }
}

4. Client Code

Uses the caretaker to manage the originator's state.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        var editor = new TextEditor();
        var caretaker = new Caretaker();

        // Initial content
        editor.Content = "Version 1";
        caretaker.Save(editor.Save());

        // Modify content
        editor.Content = "Version 2";
        caretaker.Save(editor.Save());

        // Modify content again
        editor.Content = "Version 3";
        caretaker.Save(editor.Save());

        Console.WriteLine($"Current Content: {editor.Content}");

        // Undo
        editor.Restore(caretaker.Undo());
        Console.WriteLine($"After Undo: {editor.Content}");

        // Undo again
        editor.Restore(caretaker.Undo());
        Console.WriteLine($"After Undo: {editor.Content}");

        // Redo
        editor.Restore(caretaker.Redo());
        Console.WriteLine($"After Redo: {editor.Content}");
    }
}

Output

Current Content: Version 3
After Undo: Version 2
After Undo: Version 1
After Redo: Version 2

How it works

  1. Saving State: The originator creates a memento representing its current state.
  2. Restoring State: The originator restores its state using a previously saved memento.
  3. State Management: The caretaker manages the history of mementos for undo/redo functionality.

Use cases

  1. Undo/Redo Systems: When you need to implement reversible actions.
  2. Snapshot Systems: When capturing the state of an object is required.
  3. Encapsulation: When the internal state of an object must remain private but still restorable.

Advantages

  1. Encapsulation: Keeps the originator's state private and safe from external modification.
  2. Simplified Undo/Redo: Provides a straightforward way to implement state reversal.
  3. Separation of Concerns: Decouples state management from the originator’s primary behavior.

Disadvantages

  1. Memory Overhead: Storing multiple mementos can consume significant memory for large objects.
  2. Complexity: Managing a history of mementos can introduce additional complexity.
  3. Limited Use Cases: Best suited for applications requiring state management, such as editors or workflow systems.
