Observer pattern

What it is?

The Observer pattern is a behavioral design pattern that establishes a one-to-many relationship between objects. When the subject (observable) changes its state, all dependent observers are notified and updated automatically. This pattern promotes loose coupling between the subject and its observers.


The Observer pattern:

  • Defines a dependency between objects where the subject notifies its observers of any state changes.
  • Allows for dynamic subscription and notification of events.
  • Promotes the Publish-Subscribe principle, decoupling the event producer from the event consumers.

Key components

  1. Subject (Observable): Maintains a list of observers and notifies them of state changes.
  2. Observer: Defines an interface for objects that should be notified of changes.
  3. Concrete Subject: Implements the subject interface and maintains its state.
  4. Concrete Observer: Implements the observer interface and updates itself based on changes in the subject.

Benefits

  1. Loose Coupling: Decouples subjects from observers, promoting reusability and maintainability.
  2. Dynamic Behavior: Observers can subscribe or unsubscribe at runtime.
  3. Scalability: Supports multiple observers for the same subject.

Implementation

Scenario: Stock Price Updates

1. Observer Interface

Defines the contract for all observers.

Code:

public interface IObserver
{
    void Update(string stockSymbol, double price);
}

2. Subject Interface

Defines the contract for managing observers.

Code:

public interface IStock
{
    void Attach(IObserver observer);
    void Detach(IObserver observer);
    void Notify();
}

3. Concrete Subject

Implements the subject interface and maintains its state.

Code:

public class Stock : IStock
{
    private readonly List<IObserver> _observers = new();
    public string Symbol { get; }
    public double Price { get; private set; }

    public Stock(string symbol, double price)
    {
        Symbol = symbol;
        Price = price;
    }

    public void Attach(IObserver observer)
    {
        _observers.Add(observer);
    }

    public void Detach(IObserver observer)
    {
        _observers.Remove(observer);
    }

    public void Notify()
    {
        foreach (var observer in _observers)
        {
            observer.Update(Symbol, Price);
        }
    }

    public void UpdatePrice(double newPrice)
    {
        Price = newPrice;
        Notify();
    }
}

4. Concrete Observers

Implements the observer interface to respond to notifications.

Code:

public class Investor : IObserver
{
    private readonly string _name;

    public Investor(string name)
    {
        _name = name;
    }

    public void Update(string stockSymbol, double price)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"{_name} notified: Stock {stockSymbol} price updated to {price:C}");
    }
}

5. Client Code

Demonstrates the use of the observer pattern.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        // Create stockvar appleStock = new Stock("AAPL", 150.00);

        // Create observersvar investor1 = new Investor("Alice");
        var investor2 = new Investor("Bob");

        // Attach observers
        appleStock.Attach(investor1);
        appleStock.Attach(investor2);

        // Update stock price
        appleStock.UpdatePrice(155.00);
        appleStock.UpdatePrice(160.00);

        // Detach an observer
        appleStock.Detach(investor1);

        // Update stock price again
        appleStock.UpdatePrice(165.00);
    }
}

Output

Alice notified: Stock AAPL price updated to $155.00
Bob notified: Stock AAPL price updated to $155.00
Alice notified: Stock AAPL price updated to $160.00
Bob notified: Stock AAPL price updated to $160.00
Bob notified: Stock AAPL price updated to $165.00

How it works

  1. Observer Subscription: Observers subscribe to the subject to receive updates.
  2. State Change Notification: The subject notifies all subscribed observers whenever its state changes.
  3. Dynamic Management: Observers can dynamically attach or detach at runtime.

Use cases

  1. State-Dependent Objects: When one object’s state changes should trigger updates in dependent objects.
  2. Dynamic Notification: When objects need to be dynamically added or removed from notification.
  3. Event Handling: When an event-based notification system is required.

Advantages

  1. Decoupling: Subjects and observers are loosely coupled.
  2. Flexibility: Supports dynamic subscription and unsubscription.
  3. Scalability: Allows multiple observers to be notified of state changes.

Disadvantages

  1. Potential Overhead: Notifying many observers can introduce performance overhead.
  2. Debugging Challenges: Managing dynamic subscriptions can make debugging complex.
  3. Unexpected Updates: Observers might receive updates they do not expect, leading to bugs.

  2. Notification Systems: Stock price updates, weather alerts.

State pattern

What it is?

The State pattern is a behavioral design pattern that allows an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes. It promotes encapsulation of state-specific behavior into separate classes, ensuring that the object's behavior changes dynamically depending on its state.


The State pattern:

  • Allows an object to behave differently depending on its current state.
  • Encapsulates state-specific behavior into separate classes, delegating the behavior to the current state object.
  • Promotes the Open/Closed Principle, enabling new states to be added without altering existing code.

Key characteristics

  1. Encapsulation: Encapsulates state-specific behavior into individual state classes.
  2. Dynamic Behavior: Changes the object’s behavior dynamically based on its state.
  3. Context and State Separation: Separates the logic of individual states from the context class.

Benefits

  1. Improved Readability: Encapsulating state behavior into separate classes makes the code easier to understand and maintain.
  2. Extensibility: New states can be added without modifying existing states or the context class.
  3. Eliminates Conditional Logic: Reduces large switch statements or if-else chains for state transitions.
  4. Encapsulation of State Logic: Keeps state-specific logic localized to the respective state classes.

Implementation

Scenario: A Media Player with Play, Pause, and Stop States

1. State Interface

Defines the common interface for all states.

Code:

public interface IState
{
    void Play(MediaPlayer player);
    void Pause(MediaPlayer player);
    void Stop(MediaPlayer player);
}

2. Concrete States

Implement specific behavior for each state.

Playing State:

public class PlayingState : IState
{
    public void Play(MediaPlayer player)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Already playing.");
    }

    public void Pause(MediaPlayer player)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Pausing playback.");
        player.SetState(new PausedState());
    }

    public void Stop(MediaPlayer player)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Stopping playback.");
        player.SetState(new StoppedState());
    }
}

Paused State:

public class PausedState : IState
{
    public void Play(MediaPlayer player)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Resuming playback.");
        player.SetState(new PlayingState());
    }

    public void Pause(MediaPlayer player)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Already paused.");
    }

    public void Stop(MediaPlayer player)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Stopping playback.");
        player.SetState(new StoppedState());
    }
}

Stopped State:

public class StoppedState : IState
{
    public void Play(MediaPlayer player)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Starting playback.");
        player.SetState(new PlayingState());
    }

    public void Pause(MediaPlayer player)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Cannot pause. Media is already stopped.");
    }

    public void Stop(MediaPlayer player)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Already stopped.");
    }
}

3. Context Class

Maintains a reference to the current state and delegates state-specific behavior.

Code:

public class MediaPlayer
{
    private IState _currentState;

    public MediaPlayer()
    {
        _currentState = new StoppedState(); // Default state
    }

    public void SetState(IState state)
    {
        _currentState = state;
    }

    public void Play()
    {
        _currentState.Play(this);
    }

    public void Pause()
    {
        _currentState.Pause(this);
    }

    public void Stop()
    {
        _currentState.Stop(this);
    }
}

4. Client Code

Demonstrates the state transitions and behavior.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        var player = new MediaPlayer();

        player.Play();  // Starting playback.
        player.Pause(); // Pausing playback.
        player.Play();  // Resuming playback.
        player.Stop();  // Stopping playback.
        player.Pause(); // Cannot pause. Media is already stopped.
    }
}

Output

Starting playback.
Pausing playback.
Resuming playback.
Stopping playback.
Cannot pause. Media is already stopped.

How it works

  1. State Encapsulation: Each state encapsulates its own behavior, reducing complexity in the context class.
  2. Dynamic Behavior: The context class delegates behavior to the current state object, which can change dynamically.
  3. Separation of Concerns: The context focuses on managing the state, while each state class handles its specific logic.

Use cases

  1. Dynamic Behavior: When an object’s behavior depends on its state and must change dynamically.
  2. Eliminating Conditionals: When large switch statements or if-else chains are used to manage state transitions.
  3. Complex State Logic: When state-specific behavior needs to be encapsulated and reused.

Advantages

  1. Encapsulation: Keeps state-specific logic localized to the respective classes.
  2. Extensibility: Adding new states is straightforward without modifying existing code.
  3. Clean Code: Eliminates conditional logic for state transitions, improving code readability.

Disadvantages

  1. Increased Number of Classes: Requires creating a separate class for each state, which can lead to class explosion.
  2. Complexity: May add complexity for simple state management scenarios.
  3. Overhead: The added indirection and class structure can introduce performance and maintenance overhead.

Strategy pattern

What it is?

The Strategy pattern is a behavioral design pattern that enables selecting an algorithm's behavior at runtime. It defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one in a separate class, and makes them interchangeable within their common interface.


The Strategy pattern:

  • Separates algorithm implementation from the context that uses it.
  • Promotes the Open/Closed Principle, enabling new algorithms to be added without modifying the existing code.
  • Allows behavior to be selected dynamically at runtime.

Key components

  1. Strategy Interface: Defines a common interface for all supported algorithms.
  2. Concrete Strategies: Implement the strategy interface with specific algorithms.
  3. Context: Maintains a reference to a strategy object and delegates behavior to it.

Benefits

  1. Flexibility: Allows dynamic selection of algorithms at runtime.
  2. Extensibility: Adding new algorithms is straightforward without changing existing code.
  3. Encapsulation of Algorithms: Keeps algorithm logic separate from the context, improving maintainability.
  4. Simplified Maintenance: Reduces complexity by avoiding large conditional statements.

Implementation

Scenario: Sorting Algorithms

A context can use different sorting strategies, such as QuickSort, MergeSort, or BubbleSort, based on the requirement.

1. Strategy Interface

Defines the contract for all sorting strategies.

Code:

public interface ISortStrategy
{
    void Sort(List<int> data);
}

2. Concrete Strategies

Implement specific sorting algorithms.

Quick Sort:

public class QuickSort : ISortStrategy
{
    public void Sort(List<int> data)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Using Quick Sort...");
        data.Sort(); // Simplified for demonstration
    }
}

Bubble Sort:

public class BubbleSort : ISortStrategy
{
    public void Sort(List<int> data)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Using Bubble Sort...");
        for (int i = 0; i < data.Count - 1; i++)
        {
            for (int j = 0; j < data.Count - i - 1; j++)
            {
                if (data[j] > data[j + 1])
                {
                    var temp = data[j];
                    data[j] = data[j + 1];
                    data[j + 1] = temp;
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

3. Context

Holds a reference to a strategy object and uses it to perform the algorithm.

Code:

public class SortContext
{
    private ISortStrategy _sortStrategy;

    public void SetStrategy(ISortStrategy sortStrategy)
    {
        _sortStrategy = sortStrategy;
    }

    public void ExecuteSort(List<int> data)
    {
        if (_sortStrategy == null)
        {
            throw new InvalidOperationException("Sorting strategy not set.");
        }
        _sortStrategy.Sort(data);
    }
}

4. Client Code

Demonstrates the dynamic selection of strategies.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        var data = new List<int> { 5, 2, 8, 3, 1 };

        var context = new SortContext();

        // Use Quick Sort
        context.SetStrategy(new QuickSort());
        context.ExecuteSort(data);
        Console.WriteLine($"Sorted Data: {string.Join(", ", data)}");

        // Use Bubble Sort
        data = new List<int> { 5, 2, 8, 3, 1 }; // Reset data
        context.SetStrategy(new BubbleSort());
        context.ExecuteSort(data);
        Console.WriteLine($"Sorted Data: {string.Join(", ", data)}");
    }
}

Output

Using Quick Sort...
Sorted Data: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8
Using Bubble Sort...
Sorted Data: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8

How it works

  1. Algorithm Encapsulation: Each algorithm is encapsulated in a separate class implementing the strategy interface.
  2. Dynamic Behavior: The context selects the strategy dynamically at runtime.
  3. Behavior Delegation: The context delegates the execution of the algorithm to the selected strategy.

Use cases

  1. Multiple Algorithms: When a class needs to support multiple interchangeable algorithms.
  2. Avoiding Conditionals: When large conditional statements are used to choose between algorithms.
  3. Dynamic Behavior: When the algorithm's behavior needs to change dynamically at runtime.

Advantages

  1. Extensibility: Adding new strategies does not affect existing code.
  2. Encapsulation: Keeps algorithms separate from the context.
  3. Simplified Code: Eliminates complex conditional logic in the context.
  4. Improved Testing: Each strategy can be tested independently.

Disadvantages

  1. Increased Number of Classes: Requires creating a separate class for each strategy.
  2. Context Awareness: The context must be aware of available strategies to set them appropriately.
  3. Overhead: Adds indirection, which may introduce slight performance overhead.

Template pattern

What it is?

The Template Method pattern is a behavioral design pattern that defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a base class and allows subclasses to override specific steps without altering the overall structure. It promotes code reuse and enforces a consistent structure while providing flexibility for customization.


The Template Method pattern:

  • Encapsulates the invariant parts of an algorithm in a base class.
  • Delegates the variant parts to subclasses for customization.
  • Ensures that the overall structure of the algorithm remains unchanged.

Key characteristics

  1. Skeleton of the Algorithm: Defines the structure of an algorithm in the base class.
  2. Hook Methods: Provides customizable methods for subclasses to override.
  3. Reusability: Promotes code reuse by sharing the invariant parts of the algorithm.

Benefits

  1. Code Reuse: Shares common algorithm structure between multiple implementations.
  2. Consistency: Enforces a consistent structure for all subclasses.
  3. Extensibility: Allows subclasses to provide specific implementations for certain steps.
  4. Separation of Concerns: Separates the fixed structure from the customizable steps.

Implementation

Scenario: Data Export Workflow

A data export system supports exporting data in various formats like CSV and XML. The overall workflow is the same, but the specific file format differs.

1. Abstract Base Class

Defines the template method and common steps.

Code:

public abstract class DataExporter
{
    // Template method: Defines the skeleton of the algorithmpublic void Export()
    {
        LoadData();
        FormatData();
        SaveFile();
    }

    protected abstract void LoadData();
    protected abstract void FormatData();
    protected abstract void SaveFile();
}

2. Concrete Implementations

Provide specific behavior for each step.

CSV Exporter:

public class CsvExporter : DataExporter
{
    protected override void LoadData()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Loading data for CSV export.");
    }

    protected override void FormatData()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Formatting data as CSV.");
    }

    protected override void SaveFile()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Saving data to CSV file.");
    }
}

XML Exporter:

public class XmlExporter : DataExporter
{
    protected override void LoadData()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Loading data for XML export.");
    }

    protected override void FormatData()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Formatting data as XML.");
    }

    protected override void SaveFile()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Saving data to XML file.");
    }
}

3. Client Code

Uses the template method to execute the workflow.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        // CSV Exporter
        DataExporter csvExporter = new CsvExporter();
        Console.WriteLine("CSV Export:");
        csvExporter.Export();

        Console.WriteLine();

        // XML Exporter
        DataExporter xmlExporter = new XmlExporter();
        Console.WriteLine("XML Export:");
        xmlExporter.Export();
    }
}

Output

CSV Export:
Loading data for CSV export.
Formatting data as CSV.
Saving data to CSV file.

XML Export:
Loading data for XML export.
Formatting data as XML.
Saving data to XML file.

How it works

  1. Template Method: The Export method in the base class defines the invariant structure of the algorithm.
  2. Abstract Methods: Subclasses override the abstract methods to provide specific implementations for each step.
  3. Fixed Workflow: The base class ensures that the sequence of steps in the algorithm remains consistent.

Use cases

  1. Common Algorithm Structure: When multiple classes share the same structure but require different implementations for specific steps.
  2. Consistent Workflow: When you want to enforce a consistent sequence of steps across implementations.
  3. Code Reuse: When common parts of the algorithm can be reused across multiple implementations.

Advantages

  1. Extensibility: Subclasses can customize specific steps without changing the algorithm's structure.
  2. Reusability: Shared logic is centralized in the base class.
  3. Separation of Concerns: Separates the invariant parts from the variant parts of the algorithm.
  4. Consistency: Enforces a uniform algorithm structure.

Disadvantages

  1. Increased Complexity: Adding more hooks or steps can make the base class harder to understand.
  2. Tight Coupling: Subclasses are tightly coupled to the base class, limiting flexibility.
  3. Limited Variability: The sequence of steps is fixed and cannot be easily changed without modifying the base class.

  2. Document Generation: Generating documents in different formats like PDF, DOCX, or HTML.

Visitor pattern

What it is?

The Visitor pattern is a behavioral design pattern that allows you to separate algorithms from the objects on which they operate. It introduces a way to add new behaviors to an object structure without modifying its classes, adhering to the Open/Closed Principle.


The Visitor pattern:

  • Lets you define new operations on an object structure without changing its classes.
  • Encourages the separation of behavior (visitor) from the structure (elements).
  • Promotes double dispatch, where the operation to execute is determined by both the visitor and the element it visits.

Key components

  1. Visitor Interface: Defines a common interface for all visitors.
  2. Concrete Visitors: Implement specific behaviors for different elements.
  3. Element Interface: Defines an interface for elements to accept a visitor.
  4. Concrete Elements: Represent the objects being visited.
  5. Object Structure: Holds elements and provides a way to iterate over them.

Benefits

  1. Open/Closed Principle: Allows adding new behaviors without modifying existing elements.
  2. Separation of Concerns: Decouples behaviors from the object structure.
  3. Extensibility: New visitors can be introduced without altering the object structure.

Implementation

Scenario: Tax Calculation for Products

A system needs to calculate taxes for various types of products (e.g., electronics, groceries) using different tax rules.

1. Visitor Interface

Defines the contract for all visitors.

Code:

public interface ITaxVisitor
{
    void Visit(Electronics electronics);
    void Visit(Groceries groceries);
}

2. Concrete Visitors

Implement specific tax calculation logic.

Tax Visitor:

public class TaxVisitor : ITaxVisitor
{
    public void Visit(Electronics electronics)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Electronics Tax: {electronics.Price * 0.15:C}");
    }

    public void Visit(Groceries groceries)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Groceries Tax: {groceries.Price * 0.05:C}");
    }
}

3. Element Interface

Defines the method for accepting visitors.

Code:

public interface IProduct
{
    void Accept(ITaxVisitor visitor);
    decimal Price { get; }
}

4. Concrete Elements

Represent specific product types.

Electronics:

public class Electronics : IProduct
{
    public decimal Price { get; }

    public Electronics(decimal price)
    {
        Price = price;
    }

    public void Accept(ITaxVisitor visitor)
    {
        visitor.Visit(this);
    }
}

Groceries:

public class Groceries : IProduct
{
    public decimal Price { get; }

    public Groceries(decimal price)
    {
        Price = price;
    }

    public void Accept(ITaxVisitor visitor)
    {
        visitor.Visit(this);
    }
}

5. Object Structure

Manages the collection of elements.

Code:

public class ShoppingCart
{
    private readonly List<IProduct> _products = new();

    public void AddProduct(IProduct product)
    {
        _products.Add(product);
    }

    public void ApplyTax(ITaxVisitor visitor)
    {
        foreach (var product in _products)
        {
            product.Accept(visitor);
        }
    }
}

6. Client Code

Uses the visitor to calculate taxes.

Code:

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        var cart = new ShoppingCart();

        cart.AddProduct(new Electronics(1000));
        cart.AddProduct(new Groceries(200));

        var taxVisitor = new TaxVisitor();

        Console.WriteLine("Calculating Taxes:");
        cart.ApplyTax(taxVisitor);
    }
}

Output

Calculating Taxes:
Electronics Tax: $150.00
Groceries Tax: $10.00

How it works

  1. Separation of Behavior: The visitor encapsulates behaviors (e.g., tax calculation) separate from the object structure.
  2. Double Dispatch: The Accept method in the element ensures the correct visitor method is invoked.
  3. Dynamic Extensibility: New visitors (e.g., discount calculation) can be introduced without altering the existing elements.

Use cases

  1. Complex Behaviors: When you need to add complex behaviors to an object structure without modifying the elements.
  2. Dynamic Behavior: When behaviors need to vary based on both the visitor and the element.
  3. Open/Closed Principle: When you want to add new behaviors without altering the existing codebase.

Advantages

  1. Extensibility:

    • Adding new behaviors is straightforward.

  2. Separation of Concerns:

    • Decouples object structure from behavior logic.

  3. Flexibility:

    • Enables behaviors that depend on both element types and visitor types.

Disadvantages

  1. Dependency on Element Interface: Elements must expose an Accept method, which might not always be feasible.
  2. Complexity: Adding new element types requires updating all visitors.
  3. Increased Maintenance: More classes and interfaces can increase the maintenance burden.

Examples

  1. Tax Calculation: Different tax rules for different product categories.
  2. File Processing: Performing operations like compression or encryption on different file types.
  3. Game Development: Applying different effects or actions to game objects based on their type.


Architectural


Mappers

What it is?

The Mapper pattern is a design pattern used in enterprise applications to transform data between different data models or formats. It serves as an abstraction layer that ensures the seamless conversion of data between various layers of the application, promoting separation of concerns and maintainability.


A mapper is a component responsible for:

  • Converting data from one representation to another.

  • Acting as an intermediary to facilitate data transformation between:

    • Database models and domain models.
    • Domain models and Data Transfer Objects (DTOs).
    • External API responses and internal application models.

Key characteristics

  1. Transformation: Encapsulates the logic required to convert data from one model or format to another.
  2. Abstraction: Provides a clear and consistent API for data mapping, hiding the complexities of transformation logic.
  3. Decoupling: Separates the concerns of data access, business logic, and presentation by ensuring that data transformations are managed independently.

Benefits

  1. Separation of Concerns: Keeps transformation logic separate from the domain and data access layers, resulting in cleaner, modular code.
  2. Reusability: Centralizes mapping logic, making it reusable across different parts of the application.
  3. Consistency: Ensures consistent mapping logic throughout the application.
  4. Testability: Simplifies unit testing by isolating mapping logic.

Use cases

  1. Database Model to Domain Model:

    • Transform raw database entities into rich domain objects with business logic.
    • Example: Convert a UserEntity retrieved from the database into a User domain object.

  2. Domain Model to Data Transfer Object (DTO):

    • Map domain objects to simpler DTOs for API responses or communication between layers.
    • Example: Convert a User domain object to UserDTO for a REST API response.

  3. External API to Internal Model:

    • Transform data received from an external service into a format compatible with the internal application model.

  4. Multi-Layered Systems:

    • When an application has distinct layers (e.g., presentation, business, persistence), mappers bridge the gap between them.

Implementation

1. Manual Mapping

Code Example:

public class UserMapper {

    // Map database entity to domain modelpublic static User mapToDomain(UserEntity entity) {
        return new User(entity.getId(), entity.getName(), entity.getEmail());
    }

    // Map domain model to DTOpublic static UserDTO mapToDTO(User user) {
        return new UserDTO(user.getName(), user.getEmail());
    }
}

Usage:

UserEntity entity = userRepository.findById(1L);
User domain = UserMapper.mapToDomain(entity);
UserDTO dto = UserMapper.mapToDTO(domain);

2. Using Mapping Libraries

Mapping libraries automate the transformation process, reducing boilerplate code.

  • MapStruct (Java):

    • Annotation-based library that generates mapping code at compile time.

Example:

@Mapper
public interface UserMapper {
    User toDomain(UserEntity entity);
    UserDTO toDTO(User user);
}

Generated Code: MapStruct generates the implementation automatically.

  • AutoMapper (C#):

    • A flexible, convention-based object-to-object mapper.

Example:

var config = new MapperConfiguration(cfg => {
    cfg.CreateMap<UserEntity, User>();
    cfg.CreateMap<User, UserDTO>();
});
IMapper mapper = config.CreateMapper();
User domain = mapper.Map<User>(userEntity);
UserDTO dto = mapper.Map<UserDTO>(domain);

Advanced features

  • Custom Logic: Mappers can include custom transformation logic for fields that require special handling.

Example:

@Mapper
public interface OrderMapper {
    @Mapping(source = "orderDate", target = "formattedDate", dateFormat = "dd-MM-yyyy")
    OrderDTO toDTO(Order order);
}
  • Nested Mapping: Handles mapping of nested objects or complex data structures.

Example:

public class AddressDTO {
    private String street;
    private String city;
    // Getters and Setters
}

public class UserDTO {
    private String name;
    private AddressDTO address;
    // Getters and Setters
}
  • Bidirectional Mapping: Supports mapping back and forth between models.

Challenges

  1. Complex Mapping Logic: When objects have many fields or deeply nested structures, mapping logic can become complicated.
  2. Performance Overhead: For large-scale systems, excessive mapping operations may impact performance.
  3. Maintaining Consistency: Ensuring consistency across manually written mapping logic can be error-prone.

Alternatives

  1. Direct Mapping:

    • Directly manipulate and assign values between models.
    • Drawback: Tight coupling and duplication of logic.

  2. Model Binding:

    • Framework-level solutions for binding data to models (e.g., Spring’s ModelMapper, ASP.NET’s model binding).
    • Drawback: Less explicit control over mapping logic.

Example

Scenario:

  1. The database stores user data in UserEntity.
  2. The domain layer uses User objects enriched with business logic.
  3. The API layer sends UserDTO objects in the response.

Solution:

  • Use a UserMapper to handle transformations:

    • From UserEntity to User (Database -> Domain).
    • From User to UserDTO (Domain -> API).

Code Example:

UserEntity entity = userRepository.findById(userId);
User domain = UserMapper.mapToDomain(entity);
UserDTO dto = UserMapper.mapToDTO(domain);
return ResponseEntity.ok(dto);

Best practices

  1. Centralize Mapping Logic: Keep all mapping code in dedicated mapper classes or modules.
  2. Automate with Libraries: Use tools like MapStruct or AutoMapper to reduce boilerplate.
  3. Ensure Test Coverage: Write unit tests for custom mapping logic to avoid subtle bugs.
  4. Optimize Performance: Cache or batch mapping operations for performance-critical systems.
  5. Avoid Over-Mapping: Only map the necessary fields to avoid bloated transformations.



Architectural principes

What it is?

Architectural principles refer to a set of guidelines or rules that are used to guide the design and development of a software architecture. These principles are intended to ensure that the resulting architecture is maintainable, scalable, and easy to understand and modify. Some common architectural principles include the separation of concerns, modularity, loose coupling, and high cohesion. Additionally, architectural principles are often used in conjunction with design patterns, which are reusable solutions to common software design problems.


Component principles

What it is?

Component principles in software architecture guide the design and implementation of software components, ensuring they are modular, reusable, and maintainable. These principles enhance software quality by promoting clarity, testability, and scalability while reducing complexity and the likelihood of bugs.

Characterictic

High cohesion

Cohesion refers to how closely related the responsibilities within a component are. High cohesion means that a component is focused on a single task or a closely related set of tasks.

Benefits:

  • Improves component understandability.
  • Simplifies maintenance, as related functionalities are grouped together.
  • Enhances reusability, as the component has a clear purpose.

Example:

A PaymentProcessor component should only handle payment-related tasks (e.g., validating payment details, processing payments) and not user authentication or logging.

Low coupling

Coupling refers to the degree of dependency between components. Low coupling ensures that components interact through well-defined interfaces, minimizing direct dependencies.

Benefits:

  • Reduces the impact of changes in one component on others.
  • Facilitates parallel development and testing.
  • Enhances scalability by allowing independent deployment of components.

Example:

A UserService should interact with an EmailService via an interface rather than directly depending on its implementation. This decouples their behaviors and allows the EmailService to be replaced or modified without affecting UserService.

Separation of concerns

This principle involves dividing a system into distinct areas of responsibility, ensuring that each component addresses a single concern or functionality.

Benefits:

  • Simplifies debugging and testing, as each component handles a specific concern.
  • Enhances modularity and maintainability.
  • Encourages reuse by isolating generic concerns into separate components.

Example:

In an MVC architecture:

  • The Model handles data and business logic.
  • The View manages the user interface.
  • The Controller acts as an intermediary between the Model and the View.

Interface-based design

Components should interact through well-defined interfaces rather than directly relying on each other’s implementation details.

Benefits:

  • Promotes loose coupling.
  • Makes components interchangeable.
  • Simplifies testing, as mock implementations can replace real components.

Example:

Define an IPaymentGateway interface with methods like ProcessPayment and ValidateCard. Different implementations (e.g., Stripe, PayPal) can conform to this interface without affecting the calling code.

Reusability

A reusable component can be used in multiple contexts without modification. This principle focuses on designing components with a general purpose while avoiding unnecessary dependencies.

Benefits:

  • Reduces development time by leveraging existing components.
  • Promotes consistency across projects.
  • Lowers maintenance costs.

Example:

A Logger component that supports different logging levels and formats can be reused across various applications.

Testability

Testability ensures that a component can be independently tested, both in isolation (unit testing) and as part of a larger system (integration testing).

Best Practices:

  • Avoid side effects by keeping methods deterministic.
  • Inject dependencies to simplify mocking and stubbing.
  • Use clear and minimal interfaces for interaction.

Benefits:

  • Enhances quality assurance by making it easier to identify bugs.
  • Speeds up the development process through automated testing.

Example:

A Calculator component with methods like Add, Subtract, Multiply, and Divide should return consistent outputs for the same inputs, facilitating unit testing.

Modularity

Modularity involves organizing a system into self-contained components or modules that encapsulate specific functionality.

Benefits:

  • Simplifies maintenance, as changes are confined to specific modules.
  • Enables parallel development, as teams can work on independent modules.
  • Enhances scalability, as modules can be deployed and scaled independently.

Example:

A modular e-commerce system might have separate components for ProductCatalog, OrderManagement, UserAuthentication, and PaymentProcessing.

Interoperability

Interoperability ensures that components can work together seamlessly, even if they are developed in different languages, platforms, or environments.

Best Practices:

  • Use standardized communication protocols (e.g., REST, gRPC).
  • Design components to follow common interface or data exchange standards (e.g., JSON, XML).
  • Ensure backward compatibility during updates.

Benefits:

  • Promotes integration of heterogeneous systems.
  • Reduces vendor lock-in by enabling flexibility in technology choices.

Example:

A DataService providing data via a REST API can be consumed by a frontend written in JavaScript and a backend written in Python.

Value of principles

By adhering to these principles, software systems achieve the following:

  1. Ease of Understanding: Modular components with high cohesion and clear interfaces simplify comprehension for developers.
  2. Maintainability: Low coupling and separation of concerns make changes and bug fixes easier and less risky.
  3. Reusability: Components designed for general-purpose use can be integrated into different projects or contexts.
  4. Scalability: Modular, loosely coupled systems can scale efficiently by adding or replacing components.
  5. Reliability: Interoperability and testability reduce bugs and ensure components work as expected in diverse scenarios.
  6. Cost-Effectiveness: Reusable and interoperable components save development time and resources.

Practical example

Components:

  1. UserManagement: Handles user registration and authentication.
  2. BookingService: Manages booking creation, modification, and cancellation.
  3. NotificationService: Sends email and SMS notifications.
  4. PaymentGateway: Processes payments securely.

Application of Principles:

  • High Cohesion: Each component focuses on a specific responsibility.
  • Low Coupling: Communication occurs through APIs or interfaces.
  • Separation of Concerns: Booking logic is separate from payment or notification handling.
  • Interface-Based Design: IPaymentGateway allows integration with multiple payment providers.
  • Reusability: The NotificationService can be reused in other systems.
  • Testability: Components are tested independently using mocks for external dependencies.
  • Modularity: Each component is deployed as a separate microservice.
  • Interoperability: Components communicate via REST APIs, ensuring compatibility across platforms.

Summary

Component principles in software architecture provide a blueprint for building systems that are modular, maintainable, and scalable. By incorporating these principles—such as high cohesion, low coupling, separation of concerns, and interoperability—developers can create robust systems that adapt to changing requirements while minimizing development costs and effort. These principles are the foundation of modern software design practices, ensuring quality and long-term success.


Policy vs details

What it is?

In software architecture, the distinction between policy and detail is a crucial principle that promotes the separation of concerns. This concept focuses on distinguishing high-level decisions that define the system's overall behavior (policy) from the low-level implementation choices (detail) that execute those decisions.

Policy: High-level decisions

Policy encompasses the strategic, high-level decisions that define the overall structure, behavior, and direction of the system. These decisions are typically made by architects or system designers and act as the blueprint for the system's development.

Characteristics:

  • Abstract: Focuses on the "what" and "why", not the "how".
  • Strategic: Establishes the foundation for system design and behavior.
  • Stable: Changes infrequently and drives long-term goals.

Key Examples:

  • Choosing the overall system architecture (e.g., layered architecture, microservices).
  • Defining the interfaces between major components.
  • Establishing protocols for communication between subsystems.
  • Deciding on deployment strategies (e.g., cloud-native or on-premises).
  • Selecting design patterns (e.g., MVC, Event-Driven).

Responsibility:

  • Ownership: Architects, system designers, or senior developers.
  • Impact: Sets the direction for all subsequent development work.

Detail: Low-level implementation

Detail refers to the specific, low-level implementation choices required to realize the policies. These decisions deal with the "how" of the system, focusing on the actual code, algorithms, and data structures.

Characteristics:

  • Concrete: Addresses specific implementation issues.
  • Tactical: Focused on immediate functionality and development tasks.
  • Dynamic: May change more frequently as the system evolves.

Key Examples:

  • Writing code for a RESTful API defined in the policy.
  • Selecting a specific algorithm (e.g., quicksort vs. mergesort).
  • Choosing a database engine (e.g., PostgreSQL vs. MongoDB).
  • Implementing data structures (e.g., hash tables vs. linked lists).
  • Configuring logging frameworks or CI/CD pipelines.

Responsibility:

  • Ownership: Developers or implementation teams.
  • Impact: Brings the high-level policy to life in the codebase.

Relationship between policy and detail

Dependency direction

  • Policies do not depend on details; instead, details implement policies.
  • This relationship ensures that the high-level system design remains independent of specific implementation choices, promoting flexibility and maintainability.

Analogy

  • Policy: The architect’s blueprint for a building.
  • Detail: The construction materials and techniques used by builders.

Importance of separation:

  • Flexibility: Allows developers to adapt implementation without altering the high-level design.
  • Scalability: Policies guide system growth without being tied to specific technologies.
  • Maintainability: Abstracting policies makes the system easier to update or refactor.

Policy vs. Detail in Practice

Scenario: Designing an E-Commerce Platform

  1. Policy:

    • Architecture: Use a microservices-based design.
    • Communication: RESTful APIs for inter-service communication.
    • Authentication: Implement OAuth 2.0 for user authentication.
    • Data Strategy: Separate databases for different services (e.g., orders, inventory, and users).

  2. Detail:

    • RESTful API: Implement using Spring Boot for the Order service.
    • Database: Use PostgreSQL for user data and MongoDB for product catalog.
    • Authentication: Use Keycloak to manage OAuth 2.0 tokens.
    • Caching: Implement Redis for faster inventory lookups.

Benefits

  • Clarity and Focus:

    • Policies provide a clear direction, while details handle specific implementations.
    • Developers and architects can focus on their respective areas without stepping on each other's toes.

  • Reusability:

    • Policies, such as architectural patterns or communication protocols, can be reused across different projects.
    • Details can vary while adhering to the same policy.

  • Maintainability:

    • Abstracting high-level decisions from low-level implementation makes the system easier to refactor or upgrade.

  • Flexibility:

    • Details can change (e.g., switching from one database to another) without affecting the overarching system design.

  • Testability:

    • High-level policies can be tested independently of specific implementation details.

Challenges

  • Over-Abstraction: Excessive abstraction in policy can lead to unnecessary complexity.
  • Communication Gap: Misalignment between architects (policy) and developers (detail) can cause confusion.
  • Lack of Enforcement: Without proper documentation or tooling, developers might inadvertently deviate from policy.

Tools and techniques for enforcing Policy

  1. Documentation: Clearly document policies, including architectural decisions and design principles.
  2. Code Reviews: Ensure implementation details align with the defined policies.
  3. Design Tools: Use tools like UML diagrams or architecture modeling tools to visualize policies.
  4. Static Code Analysis: Tools like SonarQube can enforce coding standards and detect violations of design principles.
  5. Automation: CI/CD pipelines can validate that implementation adheres to policies (e.g., architecture, testing requirements).

Summary

The distinction between policy and detail is a foundational principle in software architecture. Policies define the what and why at a strategic level, while details focus on the how of implementation. By maintaining a clear separation between these two layers, systems become more scalable, flexible, and maintainable. This distinction ensures that changes at the detail level do not ripple up to disrupt the overall system design, promoting a robust and future-proof architecture.


Coupling & cohesion

Introduction

Coupling and cohesion are two fundamental principles in software architecture that help define the quality and maintainability of a system. They are often used together to evaluate how well components are designed and how effectively the system is organized.

Coupling

Coupling refers to the degree of interdependence between two components in a system. It measures how much one component relies on the internal details of another.

Types (from high to low)

  1. Content Coupling (Tightest):

    • One component directly modifies or relies on the internal workings of another.
    • Example: Component A accessing private variables of Component B.

  2. Common Coupling:

    • Multiple components share global data or resources.
    • Example: Several modules accessing a global configuration variable.

  3. Control Coupling:

    • One component controls the behavior of another by passing control flags.
    • Example: A function that passes a flag to dictate what another function should do.

  4. Data Coupling:

    • Components interact by sharing only the necessary data.
    • Example: A method that accepts well-defined parameters.

  5. Message Coupling (Loosest):

    • Components communicate using abstract interfaces or messages.
    • Example: RESTful APIs where services communicate through HTTP requests.

High coupling

Characteristics:

  • Components are tightly linked.
  • Changes in one component directly affect others.
  • Testing becomes more challenging as changes propagate.

Problems:

  • Reduced modularity.
  • Increased risk of bugs when making changes.
  • Difficulty in reusing components.

Low coupling

Characteristics:

  • Components interact minimally and only through well-defined interfaces.
  • Changes in one component have little impact on others.
  • Encourages modularity and maintainability.

Benefits:

  • Easier to understand, test, and maintain.
  • Promotes component reuse.
  • Enhances scalability by enabling independent development and deployment.

Cohesion

Cohesion refers to the degree to which the responsibilities within a component are related and focused on a single purpose. It measures the "togetherness" of a component's functionality.

Types (from low to high)

  1. Coincidental Cohesion (Lowest):

    • Unrelated functionalities grouped together.
    • Example: A utility module containing logging, authentication, and database operations.

  2. Logical Cohesion:

    • Functions performing similar tasks are grouped, but they execute based on control flow.
    • Example: A function that performs all file-related operations but relies on control flags to determine specific behavior.

  3. Temporal Cohesion:

    • Functions grouped by when they are executed, not by their purpose.
    • Example: Initialization methods that perform unrelated tasks during startup.

  4. Procedural Cohesion:

    • Functions are grouped because they execute in a specific sequence.
    • Example: A workflow module combining steps for order processing.

  5. Communicational Cohesion:

    • Functions operate on the same data or contribute to the same output.
    • Example: A component that processes and formats user input.

  6. Functional Cohesion (Highest):

    • Every responsibility contributes directly to a single, well-defined purpose.
    • Example: A PaymentProcessor class that validates, processes, and logs payments.

High cohesion

Characteristics:

  • All functionalities within a component are tightly related to its purpose.
  • Clear, well-defined responsibilities.
  • Easier to understand, test, and maintain.

Benefits:

  • Improves readability and modularity.
  • Simplifies debugging and testing.
  • Promotes reuse by clearly defining the component’s functionality.

Low cohesion

  • Characteristics:

    • Responsibilities within a component are unrelated or loosely related.
    • Components become overly complex and difficult to understand.

  • Problems:

    • Reduced maintainability.
    • Increased likelihood of bugs.
    • Harder to test as unrelated responsibilities are bundled together.

Coupling and cohesion comparison

Aspect

High Coupling

Low Coupling

High Cohesion

Low Cohesion

Dependency

Strong interdependence between components

Minimal interdependence

Tight focus on a single purpose

Scattered responsibilities

Change Impact

Changes propagate across components

Changes are isolated to specific components

Localized changes

Changes affect multiple unrelated functions

Testability

Difficult to test components independently

Easy to test components independently

Easier to test and debug

Hard to test due to unrelated responsibilities

Reusability

Difficult to reuse components

High potential for reuse

Clear, reusable components

Rarely reusable due to unclear responsibilities

Maintenance

High risk of introducing bugs

Easier to maintain

Simplifies maintenance

Maintenance is complex

Examples

Low Coupling, High Cohesion:

  • Scenario: A microservices architecture.

    • Services like UserService, OrderService, and PaymentService have:

      • Low Coupling: Interact only via APIs.
      • High Cohesion: Each service focuses on its domain-specific responsibilities.

High Coupling, Low Cohesion:

  • Scenario: A monolithic application with tightly intertwined modules.

    • High Coupling: Changes in one module require updates in others.
    • Low Cohesion: Modules handle multiple unrelated tasks (e.g., a single module managing UI rendering, data access, and business logic).

Best practices

  1. Aim for Low Coupling and High Cohesion: Design components to have minimal dependencies and well-defined responsibilities.
  2. Use Interface-Based Design: Define interactions through interfaces to reduce coupling.
  3. Encapsulate Responsibilities: Group related functionalities and data within a single component.
  4. Refactor Regularly: Identify and address high coupling or low cohesion in code.
  5. Use Dependency Injection: Decouple component dependencies and make them configurable.
  6. Adopt Design Patterns: Patterns like Factory, Mediator, and Observer help achieve low coupling.
  7. Modular Architecture: Use architectural styles like microservices or layered architecture to enforce separation of concerns.

Key Takeaways

  • Coupling measures how much components depend on each other: Aim for low coupling to promote modularity and ease of maintenance.
  • Cohesion measures how well a component's responsibilities align: Aim for high cohesion to ensure components are focused and understandable.
  • Balancing low coupling with high cohesion results in systems that are scalable, maintainable, and resilient to change.



Boundries

Introduction

Boundaries in software architecture refer to the interfaces or points of separation between different components, modules, or systems. They serve as lines of interaction that define how various parts of a system communicate while maintaining independence. Boundaries can be physical (e.g., between services in a distributed system) or logical (e.g., between layers in an application).

Importance

Defining boundaries is critical for creating scalable, maintainable, and modular systems. Clear boundaries:

  1. Promote Modularity: Components with well-defined boundaries can be developed, tested, and maintained independently.
  2. Simplify Communication: By specifying interaction points, boundaries make communication between components predictable and structured.
  3. Facilitate Understanding: Clear separation of concerns makes the system easier to understand for developers and stakeholders.
  4. Support Scalability: Boundaries enable components to scale independently, whether vertically (adding resources) or horizontally (adding instances).
  5. Enhance Testability: Well-defined boundaries allow for targeted testing of individual components without needing the entire system.
  6. Enable Reusability: Components with clear boundaries can be reused in other contexts or systems.

Types

Physical boundaries

These boundaries separate components or systems deployed on different physical infrastructure.

Examples:

  • Microservices deployed in separate containers or servers.
  • Different databases for separate domains in a system.

Key Characteristics:

  • Often enforced by the network layer (e.g., REST APIs, message queues).
  • Designed to handle system distribution and scalability.

Logical boundaries

Logical boundaries divide responsibilities within a single system, typically within the same physical deployment.

Examples:

  • Separation between the presentation layer, business logic layer, and data access layer in a layered architecture.
  • Bounded contexts in Domain-Driven Design.

Key characteristics:

  • Enforced through code structure, interfaces, or modules.
  • Promote separation of concerns and better system organization.

Design principles

Explicit interfaces

Every boundary should have a clear and well-defined interface to facilitate communication.

Benefits:

  • Prevents components from relying on internal details of others.
  • Simplifies future changes and integrations.

Example:

  • A UserService exposes a RESTful API for creating and fetching user data.

Loose coupling

Boundaries should minimize dependencies between components.

Benefits:

  • Changes in one component do not ripple across the entire system.

Example:

  • A payment service interacts with an order service only via API calls, not by directly accessing its database.

Encapsulation

Internal implementation details of a component should not be exposed across boundaries.

Benefits:

  • Protects the integrity of components and prevents unintended interactions.

Example:

  • A microservice exposes only specific endpoints and hides internal logic from external systems.

Separation of concerns

Responsibilities are distributed across components, each focused on a specific concern.

Benefits:

  • Simplifies debugging, testing, and development.

Example:

  • A frontend interacts with a backend service to fetch data but doesn’t manage database access.

Consistency and standardization

Boundaries should follow consistent conventions for easier integration.

Benefits:

  • Reduces complexity in cross-boundary communication.

Example:

  • Using consistent API standards like REST or GraphQL across services.

Common scenarios

Microservices architecture

Physical boundaries between microservices, often communicating through APIs or message brokers.

Challenges:

  • Managing distributed systems and network latency.
  • Ensuring secure and reliable communication.

Layered architecture

Logical boundaries between layers such as presentation, business logic, and data access.

Challenges:

  • Avoiding tight coupling between layers.
  • Maintaining clear separation of responsibilities.

Bounded contexts in Domain-Driven Design

Logical boundaries around domain-specific models.

Challenges:

  • Defining clear integration points between contexts.
  • Handling data consistency across boundaries.

Benefits

  1. Improved Modularity: Components can be updated or replaced without affecting others.
  2. Better Scalability: Services or components can scale independently based on demand.
  3. Enhanced Security: Boundaries act as barriers to restrict unauthorized access.
  4. Ease of Maintenance: Clear responsibilities reduce complexity when debugging or adding features.
  5. Team Autonomy: Different teams can work on separate components without interfering with each other.

Challenges

  1. Overlapping Responsibilities: Poorly defined boundaries can lead to duplicated functionality or unclear ownership.
  2. Communication Overhead: Excessive boundaries (e.g., too many microservices) can increase communication complexity.
  3. Dependency Management: Incorrectly handled dependencies can lead to tight coupling between components.
  4. Boundary Evolution: As requirements change, boundaries may need to be redefined, which can be complex.

Example

Boundaries in Practice:

  1. Microservices:

    • Physical boundaries between services like OrderService, PaymentService, and InventoryService.

  2. Layers:

    • Logical boundaries between the frontend, backend, and database.

  3. API Gateways:

    • Acts as a boundary between external clients and internal microservices.

Boundary Design:

  • Use REST APIs for communication between microservices.
  • Ensure each microservice has clear ownership of its data.
  • Decouple frontend and backend with a shared API contract.

Tools and practices for managing boundaries

  1. Documentation: Define interfaces and interaction protocols for all boundaries.
  2. API Management Tools: Tools like Postman, Swagger, or Apigee for managing and testing API boundaries.
  3. Monitoring and Logging: Tools like Prometheus, Grafana, or ELK Stack to observe interactions across boundaries.
  4. Integration Tests: Test communication between components to validate boundary correctness.
  5. Boundary-Oriented Design Techniques: Use techniques like EventStorming or Context Mapping to define clear boundaries.

Summary

Boundaries in software architecture are vital for organizing systems into modular, maintainable, and scalable components. By clearly defining boundaries—whether physical (e.g., microservices) or logical (e.g., layers or bounded contexts)—architects ensure that components interact predictably while remaining independent. Properly managed boundaries lead to systems that are easier to test, maintain, and evolve, reducing complexity and promoting reusability.



API


Security

API secruity

APIs are the backbone of modern applications. They expose a very large surface area for attacks, increasing the risk of security vulnerabilities. Common threats include SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks. 



Study cases


How Facebook served billions of requests per second Using Memcached

There are two absolute truths about running a social network at the scale of Facebook:

  • First, it cannot go down.
  • Second, it cannot run slow.

These two factors determine whether people are going to stay on your social network or not. 


Even a few people leaving impacts the entire user base because the users are interconnected. Most people are online because their friends or relatives are online and there’s a domino effect at play. If one user drops off due to issues, there are chances that other users will also leave. Facebook had to deal with these issues early on because of its popularity. At any point in time, millions of people were accessing Facebook from all over the world.


In terms of software design, this meant a few important requirements:

  • Facebook had to support real-time communication.
  • They had to build capabilities for on-the-fly content aggregation.
  • Scale to handle billions of user requests.
  • Store trillions of items across multiple geographic locations.

To achieve these goals, Facebook took up the open-source version of Memcached and enhanced it to build a distributed key-value store. This enhanced version was known as Memcache.


Introduction to Memcached

Memcached is an in-memory key-value store that supports a simple set of operations such as set, get, and delete.

The open-source version provided a single-machine in-memory hash table. The engineers at Facebook took up this version as a basic building block to create a distributed key-value store known as Memcache.In other words, “Memcached” is the source code or the running binary whereas “Memcache” stands for the distributed system behind it. Technically, Facebook used Memcache in two main ways:

Query Cache

The job of the query cache was to reduce the load on the primary source-of-truth databases.

In this mode, Facebook used Memcache as a demand-filled look-aside cache. You may have also heard about it as the cache-aside pattern. The below diagram shows how the look-aside cache pattern works for the read and write path.

The read path utilizes a cache that is filled on-demand. This means that data is only loaded into the cache when a client specifically requests it. 


Before serving the request, the client first checks the cache. If the desired data is not found in the cache (a cache miss), the client retrieves the data from the database and also updates the cache.

The write path takes a more interesting approach to updating data. 


After a particular key is updated in the database, the system doesn’t directly update the corresponding value in the cache. Instead, it removes the data for that key from the cache entirely. This process is known as cache invalidation.


By invalidating the cache entry, the system ensures that the next time a client requests data for that key, it will experience a cache miss and be forced to retrieve the most up-to-date value directly from the database. This approach helps maintain data consistency between the cache and the database.

Generic Cache

Facebook also leverages Memcache as a general-purpose key-value store. This allows different teams within the organization to utilize Memcache for storing pre-computed results generated from computationally expensive machine learning algorithms.

By storing these pre-computed ML results in Memcache, other applications can quickly and easily access them whenever needed.

This approach offers several benefits such as improved performance and resource optimization.

High-Level Architecture of Facebook

Facebook’s architecture is built to handle the massive scale and global reach of its platform. 

At the time of their Memcached adoption, Facebook’s high-level architecture consisted of three key components:

1 - Regions

Facebook strategically places its servers in various locations worldwide, known as regions. These regions are classified into two types:

  • Primary Region: The primary region is responsible for handling the majority of user traffic and data management.
  • Secondary Region: Multiple secondary regions are distributed globally to provide redundancy, load balancing, and improved performance for users in different geographical areas.

Each region, whether primary or secondary, contains multiple frontend clusters and a single storage cluster.

2 - Frontend Clusters

Within each region, Facebook employs frontend clusters to handle user requests and serve content. A frontend cluster consists of two main components:

  • Web Servers: These servers are responsible for processing user requests, rendering pages, and delivering content to the users.
  • Memcache Servers: Memcache servers act as a distributed caching layer, storing frequently accessed data in memory for quick retrieval.

The frontend clusters are designed to scale horizontally based on demand. As user traffic increases, additional web and Memcache servers can be added to the cluster to handle the increased load.

3 - Storage Cluster

At the core of each region lies the storage cluster. This cluster contains the source-of-truth database, which stores the authoritative copy of every data item within Facebook’s system. The storage cluster takes care of data consistency, durability, and reliability. By replicating data across multiple regions and employing a primary-secondary architecture, Facebook achieves high availability and fault tolerance.


The below diagram shows the high-level view of this architecture:

One major philosophy that Facebook adopted was a willingness to expose slightly stale data instead of allowing excessive load on the backend. 

Rather than striving for perfect data consistency at all times, Facebook accepted that users may sometimes see outdated information in their feeds. This approach allowed them to handle high traffic loads without crumbling under excessive strain on the backend infrastructure.

To make this architecture work at an unprecedented scale of billions of requests every day, Facebook had to solve multiple challenges such as:

  • Managing latency and failures within a cluster.
  • Managing data replication within a region.
  • Managing data consistency across regions.

In the next few sections, we will look at how Facebook handled each of these challenges.

Within Cluster Challenges

There were three important goals for the within-cluster operations:

  • Reducing latency
  • Reducing the load on the database
  • Handling failures

1 - Reducing Latency

As mentioned earlier, every frontend cluster contains hundreds of Memcached servers, and items are distributed across these servers using techniques like Consistent Hashing.

For reference, Consistent Hashing is a technique that allows the distribution of a set of keys across multiple nodes in a way that minimizes the impact of node failures or additions. When a node goes down or a new node is introduced, Consistent Hashing ensures that only a small subset of keys needs to be redistributed, rather than requiring a complete reshuffling of data.

The diagram illustrates the concept of Consistent Hashing where keys are mapped to a circular hash space, and nodes are assigned positions on the circle. Each key is assigned to the node that falls closest to it in a clockwise direction.



At Facebook's scale, a single web request can trigger hundreds of fetch requests to retrieve data from Memcached servers. Consider a scenario where a user loads a popular page containing numerous posts and comments. 

Even a single request can require the web servers to communicate with multiple Memcached servers in a short timeframe to populate the necessary data.

This high-volume data fetching occurs not only in cache hit situations but also when there’s a cache miss. The implication is that a single Memcached server can turn into a bottleneck for many web servers, leading to increased latency and degraded performance for the end user.

To reduce the possibility of such a scenario, Facebook uses a couple of important tricks visualized in the diagram.



Parallel Requests and Batching

To understand the concept of parallel requests and batching, consider a simple analogy. 

Imagine going to the supermarket every time you need an item. It would be incredibly time-consuming and inefficient to make multiple trips for individual items. Instead, it’s much more effective to plan your shopping trip and purchase a bunch of items together in a single visit.

The same optimization principle applies to data retrieval in Facebook's frontend clusters. 

To maximize the efficiency of data retrieval, Facebook constructs a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) that represents the dependencies between different data items.

The DAG provides a clear understanding of which data items can be fetched concurrently and which items depend on others.

By analyzing the DAG, the web server can determine the optimal order and grouping of data fetches. It identifies data items that can be retrieved in parallel, without any dependencies, and groups them in a single batch request.

Using UDP 

Facebook employed a clever strategy to optimize network communication between the web servers and the Memcache server.

For fetch requests, Facebook configured the clients to use UDP instead of TCP. 

As you may know, UDP is a connectionless protocol and much faster than TCP. By using UDP, the clients can send fetch requests to the Memcache servers with less network overhead, resulting in faster request processing and reduced latency.

However, UDP has a drawback: it doesn’t guarantee the delivery of packets. If a packet is lost during transmission, UDP doesn’t have a built-in mechanism to retransmit it. 

To handle such cases, they treated UDP packet loss as a cache miss on the client side. If a response isn’t received within a specific timeframe, the client assumes that the data is not available in the cache and proceeds to fetch it from the primary data source.

For update and delete operations, Facebook still used TCP since it provided a reliable communication channel that ensured the delivery of packets in the correct order. It removed the need for adding a specific retry mechanism, which is important when dealing with update and delete operations.

All these requests go through a special proxy known as mcrouter that runs on the same machine as the webserver. Think of the mcrouter as a middleman that performs multiple duties such as data serialization, compression, routing, batching, and error handling. We will look at mcrouter in a later section.

2 - Reducing Load

The most important goal for Memcache is to reduce the load on the database by reducing the frequency of data fetching from the database. 

Using Memcache as a look-aside cache solves this problem significantly. But at Facebook’s scale, two caching-related issues can easily appear.

  • Stale Set: This happens when the cache is set with outdated data and there’s no easy way of invalidating it.
  • Thundering Herd: This problem occurs in a highly concurrent environment when a cache miss triggers a thundering herd of requests to the database.

The below diagram visualizes both of these issues.



To minimize the probability of these two critical issues, Facebook used a technique known as leasing.

Leasing helped solve both stale sets and thundering herds, helping Facebook reduce peak DB query rates from 17K/second to 1.3K/second.

Stale Sets

Consider that a client requests memcache for a particular key and it results in a cache miss.

Now, it’s the client’s responsibility to fetch the data from the database and also update memcache so that future requests for the same key don’t result in a cache miss.

This works fine most of the time but in a highly concurrent environment, the data being set by the client may get outdated by the time it gets updated in the cache.

Leasing prevents this from happening. 

With leasing, Memcache hands over a lease (a 64-bit token bound to a specific key) to a particular client to set data into the cache whenever there’s a cache miss. 

The client has to provide this token when setting the value in the cache and memcache can verify whether the data should be stored by verifying the token. If the item was already invalidated by the time the client tried to update, Memcache will invalidate the lease token and reject the request.

The below diagram shows the concept of leasing in a much better manner.



Thundering Herds

A slight modification to the leasing technique also helps solve the thundering herd issue.

In this modification, Memcache regulates the rate of issuing the lease tokens. For example, it may return a token once every 5 seconds per key.

For any requests for the key within 5 seconds of the lease token being issued, Memcache sends a special response requesting the client to wait and retry so that these requests don’t hit the database needlessly. This is because there’s a high probability that the client holding the lease token will soon update the cache and the waiting clients will get a cache hit when they retry.


Reddit architecture

Architecture

The main points of Reddit’s architecture are as follows:

  1. Reddit uses a Content Delivery Network (CDN) from Fastly as a front for the application
  2. Reddit started using jQuery in early 2009. Later on, they started using Typescript and have now moved to modern Node.js frameworks. Over the years, Reddit has also built mobile apps for Android and iOS.
  3. Within the application stack, the load balancer sits in front and routes incoming requests to the appropriate services.
  4. Reddit started as a Python-based monolithic application but has since started moving to microservices built using Go.
  5. Reddit heavily uses GraphQL for its API layer. In early 2021, they started moving to GraphQL Federation, which is a way to combine multiple smaller GraphQL APIs known as Domain Graph Services (DGS). In 2022, the GraphQL team at Reddit added several new Go subgraphs for core Reddit entities thereby splitting the GraphQL monolith.
  6. From a data storage point of view, Reddit relies on Postgres for its core data model. To reduce the load on the database, they use memcached in front of Postgres. Also, they use Cassandra quite heavily for new features mainly because of its resiliency and availability properties.
  7. To support data replication and maintain cache consistency, Reddit uses Debezium to run a Change Data Capture process.
  8. Expensive operations such as a user voting or submitting a link are deferred to an async job queue via RabbitMQ and processed by job workers. For content safety checks and moderation, they use Kafka to transfer data in real-time to run rules over them.
  9. Reddit uses AWS and Kubernetes as the hosting platform for its various apps and internal services.
  10. For deployment and infrastructure, they use Spinnaker, Drone CI, and Terraform.


Technologies


Dapr

What it is?

Dapr is a portable, event-driven runtime that exposes standardized, language-agnostic APIs (“building blocks”) for common distributed-systems concerns—service-to-service calls, pub/sub, state, workflow, actors, secrets, config, bindings, resiliency, and observability—implemented via a sidecar process you call over HTTP/gRPC.

Why use

  • Productivity & portability. Call POST /v1.0/state/... or .../invoke/... and switch implementations (Redis↔Cosmos DB, Kafka↔RabbitMQ, etc.) without changing app code; you only swap Dapr components (YAML).
  • Polyglot by design. Any language that can speak HTTP/gRPC works (SDKs for .NET, Go, Java, Python, JS, etc.).
  • Built-in resilience, security, and telemetry. mTLS with a built-in CA (Sentry), SPIFFE identities, configurable retries/timeouts/circuit breakers, and native OpenTelemetry tracing.
  • Cloud and edge, self-hosted or Kubernetes, and first-class integration in Azure Container Apps.

Architecture

  • Sidecar pattern: each app instance runs daprd alongside your process; your code calls the sidecar, and the sidecar talks to state stores, brokers, etc. On Kubernetes, the sidecar injector adds daprd to annotated pods.
  • Building blocks (APIs): Service Invocation, Pub/Sub, State, Actors, Bindings, Secrets, Configuration, Workflow, Jobs (scheduling), plus cross-cutting Resiliency and Observability. You can adopt them independently.
  • Components: pluggable adapters (YAML) that connect a building block to a concrete backend (Redis, Cosmos DB, DynamoDB; Kafka, RabbitMQ; Key Vault, Vault, etc.). Each component has a maturity level (alpha/beta/stable).

Building blocks

Service Invocation

Direct, secure service-to-service calls with service discovery, retries, and timeouts handled by Dapr.

Invoke URL pattern (HTTP):

POST http://localhost:3500/v1.0/invoke/{app-id}/method/{path}

Publish/Subscribe

Topic-based messaging with CloudEvents envelopes; swap brokers without code changes (Kafka, RabbitMQ, Redis Streams, Pulsar, AWS SNS/SQS, Azure Event Hubs/Service Bus, GCP Pub/Sub, etc.).

State Management

Key/value state with ETags & transactions across a variety of stores (Redis, Cosmos DB, DynamoDB, Cassandra, MongoDB, etc.).

Actors (Virtual Actors)

Per-ID single-threaded “grains” with timers/reminders and durable state, implemented over the state building block.

Bindings

Input/output bindings to external systems (including Cron as an input binding to trigger code on a schedule).

Secrets

Uniform API to retrieve secrets from providers like Kubernetes, Vault, Azure Key Vault; you can reference secrets in component YAMLs.

Configuration

Read-only key/value config with change subscriptions; separate from sidecar/control-plane configuration.

Workflow

In-sidecar workflow runtime; author workflows in code, manage via HTTP/gRPC; built atop Actors for durability.

Jobs (scheduling)

Schedule “do X at time T or every N minutes”; powered by the Scheduler control-plane service; currently maturing.

Resiliency & Observability

Declarative timeouts, retries, circuit breakers; distributed tracing via OpenTelemetry/OTLP (plus Zipkin).

Security model

mTLS by default between sidecars (Sentry = CA); each app gets a SPIFFE ID (spiffe://<trustdomain>/ns/<namespace>/<appid>). You can add invoke ACLs.

Comparison with other solutions

  • Versus a service mesh: Both use sidecars, both can do mTLS and tracing, but Dapr is an app runtime (APIs for state/pubsub/etc.), not a networking mesh. They’re complementary and often run together.
  • Versus hand-rolled libs/SDKs: You avoid provider lock-in and duplicated boilerplate; you trade that for learning Dapr and operating sidecars.

Use cases

  • Polyglot microservices where teams don’t want to bake cloud-specific SDKs into code.
  • Event-driven systems (pub/sub) with multiple brokers across environments.
  • Stateful services needing idempotency, concurrency control (ETags), and virtual actors.
  • Edge + cloud deployments and Azure Container Apps scenarios with managed Dapr.

Pros & cons

Pros

  • Standardized APIs for cross-cutting concerns; language & platform neutral.
  • Swappable providers via components ⇒ less lock-in, faster experiments.
  • Built-in resilience/telemetry/security (mTLS, retries, timeouts, circuit breakers, OTLP tracing).
  • Actors & Workflow for durable, long-running processes.

Cons

  • Sidecar overhead (extra container/process per app), memory/CPU and ops complexity; if you also run a service mesh, consider combined overhead and operational surface.
  • Component maturity varies (alpha/beta/stable) — verify status for your chosen store/broker.
  • Learning curve & debugging through an abstraction; must understand both Dapr and your underlying backends.
  • Feature fit: some advanced, provider-specific features may still require direct SDKs.
